#6515. NASA Warns a Monster El Niño Could Surpass the Historic 1997 Event

An El Niño that could beat 1997’s record is taking shape in the Pacific, leaving scientists watching for its next move.

El Niño is part of a natural climate pattern that returns roughly every two to seven years. Its most recent very strong events, in 1997–98 and 2015–16, disrupted weather worldwide. Consequences included fires in Indonesia and the Amazon, crop failures caused by drought in southern Africa, and heavy rain and coastal flooding in Southern California.

Satellite measurements show that the current El Niño resembles the 1997–98 event, with warm water stretching across the equatorial Pacific to South America. But that oceanic resemblance does not guarantee the same weather during winter 2026–27, as the outcome also depends on how the atmosphere responds.

Every El Niño starts with a change in the tropical Pacific’s winds. Trade winds normally push warm surface water westward, leaving sea levels higher in the western Pacific than in the east. When those winds weaken, warm water begins moving back toward the central and eastern Pacific.

As warmth spreads eastward, the trade winds weaken further and sometimes reverse, allowing still more warm water to follow. This feedback loop helps El Niño intensify.

But strength alone does not determine its effects. The location of the warmest water and the atmosphere’s response also shape the outcome. “The search for the ‘typical’ El Niño is very elusive,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). “They’re all different in terms of where they land and how their impacts play out.”

Scientists can track that developing pattern from space because warming water expands, raising the sea surface. Across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, unusually high water therefore provides a signal of El Niño’s heat buildup.

The maps compare sea surface height anomalies on October 13, 1997 (left), and October 12, 2026 (right). JPL scientists processed measurements from TOPEX/Poseidon and Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich, respectively. Red shows higher-than-average sea levels, white indicates normal conditions, and blue marks lower levels. Seasonal effects and long-term trends have been removed to highlight El Niño and other short-term natural changes.

“What’s unique about altimetry is that we have a 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying almost the same ground track, with each mission overlapping the next,” Willis said. “That lets us look back in time and compare this El Niño to what happened in 1997. And right now, this one is on track to be even bigger.”

Although the 2026 El Niño developed much more abruptly, by October it shared two defining features with 1997: lower sea levels in the west and higher levels in the east, with warm, elevated water reaching South America. Willis thinks that resemblance could translate into similar impacts, including the abundant rainfall seen across California and the southern United States in 1997–98.

The powerful 2015–16 event shows why the arrangement of that heat matters. A map based on Jason-2 measurements from October 12, 2015, appears alongside the 1997 and 2026 comparisons. In 2015, the exceptionally warm, high water along the equator did not reach as far against South America. That winter, rainfall effects were concentrated more over Central America and the southeastern United States, with significant flooding in Mexico.

NOAA’s October 8, 2026, El Niño outlook assigned an 83 percent chance of a strong to very strong event through the first three months of 2027. Still, its effects during winter 2026–27 and beyond remain uncertain. El Niño’s influence passes through a chaotic atmosphere, and its signal becomes harder to distinguish beyond the tropics.

“There’s always a bit of a dice roll here,” Willis said. “Just because this El Niño looks like 1997 doesn’t mean it will be exactly the same—it’s just our best guess at the moment.”

The place that I record every second (every second!), at any moment of the day, on the dial of a clock—a mechanism that, just as reliably and accurately, always measures every step on this part of the Earth, every moment of our lives, and also measures the static (standard) length of this rotation of the Earth (a day!), all its 86,400 parts (moments of existence), and arranges them not in a stack, not in a bag, not even in a file, but in a circular row on the clock’s dial—as a record of all the minutes and hours of the day—measures! And the big hand of the clock (at this moment!) points to the place in the day (the point, the moment of this day) where I (and the whole world!) am, where I am living now!. A second is an empty, old word, a mistaken concept, because in the dark ages it measured not BEING, not life, but the “time” invented by the pharaohs and philosophers of Babylon — which, of course, was not real, visible, obvious, or understandable! If the measures “gram” or “meter” are real, obvious, understandable, and consistent in weight or length, then “second” has never even seen WHAT it measures, is not even familiar with the word “time,” and is not friends with anyone; it exists indifferently, uninterestingly, boringly—after all, it is a measure shaped, measured, and created by human hands?! An unnoticed, indispensable worker. A second – it doesn’t rush, doesn’t hurry, doesn’t push, doesn’t drag on, doesn’t stretch, doesn’t accelerate; it’s not relative (doesn’t relate) to anything (just like a centimeter or a 1‑kilogram weight), it doesn’t fly, doesn’t have a direction or speed… just like the measures “minute,” “hour,” “day,” “year”! There is: her short, small length, which imperceptibly, non‑stop, and coolly measures, records, sets aside, and files every moment of life into the “minute” file. It doesn’t care whether a turtle is crawling or a bison is fleeing in fear. But it always informs every person, provides invaluable information: “You are not making it by the end of the day, by the deadline; you are running late!” A second measures existence, my sleep, all the events of the universe! Here is the Truth: “A second is the measure of life!” It doesn’t get along with, isn’t even familiar with the empty word “time.” It is Man himself who assigns and uses it — the same measure to measure different (all) moments of life! Unlike the word “time” (an ancient fake created by power and religion), a second is material, real (and not just the mechanism of the alarm clock itself!), obvious, understandable; it can be filled with a clap, the sound of music, a voice, and even the Beat of the Heart (the prototype of a second), the pulse of a living person! A second is a measure of life (of all episodes of life!) and a measure of this day! A measure of measuring a part, a segment of eternal existence. A second is a real, noticeable, obvious, eternal, static measure created by us to measure life: the life of a person, a planet, a country, a frog, a dolphin! A second is a measure of all events, activities, their duration, their beginning and end, their place in the queue, in the chaos, surrounded by other events on the “event timeline of this day”! This is how we get (have) a clear order of things and notice, mark (take into account!) The causes and effects of all phenomena and events, their “cause-and-effect” relationships! Only the quick-witted, hasty astrophysicists of the planet lack logic in their fabrication about the nature of the “singular point” of the Big Bang; they have neither a cause nor an explanation or understanding of the central falsification of their Theory of Everything!? Seconds add up, filling the measures: minute, hour, day (twenty‑four hours), and days (a day is the Earth’s rotation) fill the “files of life measurement”: week, month, year! It is because of the mistakes made by these scientists that we, you and I, end up with the “MAIN QUESTION OF COSMOLOGY” from Wikipedia, and its main error: “How did the Universe come into being?”!??.. But this idea is precisely the cause of all the troubles on the planet, the reason for the emergence of millions of fake dissertations, publications, and theories from organized, powerful groups. After all, it is obvious and likely that the emptiness of space is ETERNAL, just like its adornment; the meaning and purpose of its existence a MAN — or, more precisely, humanity as a whole!

“Scientists can track that developing pattern from space because warming water expands, raising the sea surface.”

The sea surface is moved by tides, drifting air masses with different pressures, prevailing winds, random gusts, constructive interference of waves from all over the world, and ubiquitous, local waves. Those influences, many with short temporal duration, have to be averaged to obtain an estimate of the mean surface elevation. I have never seen an estimate of the standard deviation, often used as an estimate for the uncertainty of the mean. Things like “rogue waves,” (constructive/destructive interference) are probably usually missed, despite their great height, because of their short duration and narrow width.

Why the preference for altimetry instead of a direct measure of temperature? Because of surface mixing and the thermal inertia of water, it would seem to me that thermal IR would be a more direct measurement of the influence of El Niño on weather.

Once again, it appears necessary to remind these authors, and others, that “could” is a qualitative, not quantitative, word used to describe a low-probability event that is not, however, impossible. That is, it is permissive, not obligatory. In fact, the way it is commonly used, it has less probability of occurring than not occurring. Given that it is not associated with a numeric probability, there isn’t much else about it that can be said that is actionable. It is a word best used by a defense attorney trying to convince a jury that it is possible that his/her client is innocent of the charges brought. Our jurisprudence system is purposely designed to minimize wrongful convictions. It is embodied in the guiding principle that it is better that 10 guilty criminals are set free rather than one innocent person be punished. Science is not supposed to have such biases.

If this developing El Niño turns out to not be as strong or long-lasting as it ‘could’ be, will we hear any more about it after the fact? Will we get an explanation for why it didn’t live up to the arm waving? Probably not, because meteorologists don’t really know what triggers an El Niño. About the best they can do is predict that they will occur episodically every two to seven years. They are like a great earthquake or volcanic eruption in that respect.

#6514. Goat Kari

Food writer Rachel Gurjar made this goat kari for her “lifelong idol” Madhur Jaffrey, the renowned Indian cookbook author, at a dinner Gurjar hosted in her Brooklyn apartment in September 2022. When Jaffrey asked for the recipe, Gurjar knew she had to include it in her debut cookbook, East to East.

You can find goat meat at your local halal butcher or substitute lamb. If opting for goat, Gurjar recommends requesting a bone-in “curry cut,” which means the butcher will cut the meat into 2- to 3-inch pieces that are ideal for braising.

While you can use store-bought garam masala, Gurjar always DIYs her own spice blend inspired by the one her mother used to make back in India. “It’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional,” she writes. “This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again.” You can also customize your blend: Add more cinnamon and fennel for a sweeter garam masala, or up the black pepper and cloves for a spicier kick.

#6512. Antarctica’s Melting Ice Has Triggered a Sudden Shift Deep in the Ocean

Ocean measurements show a vast Southern Hemisphere water layer growing saltier and denser, a shift that could send more heat into deep waters than climate models predict.

Every Antarctic summer, melting sea ice sends a vast pulse of fresh water into the ocean. That seasonal supply helps sustain Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW), a layer of relatively fresh seawater that spreads across much of the Southern Hemisphere’s ocean. The AAIW helps store carbon, supply oxygen, and drive global currents, redistributing heat, fresh water, and carbon around the planet.

From 1995 to 2015, summer ice melt helped maintain this layer. But from 2016 to 2024, reduced freshwater input left it saltier, denser, and deeper, abruptly reversing its long-term trends in salinity, or salt content, and density.

The findings, published in Nature Climate Change, provide the first direct observational evidence of this change in the AAIW’s properties. The international research team analyzed data from the global Argo program, a network of around 4,000 robotic floats that sample the upper oceans, alongside satellite and atmospheric datasets.

The study was led by Associate Professor Bishakhdatta Gayen, of the University of Melbourne and the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), and Kaushik Mishra, a PhD student at IISc. Gayen said:

“The Antarctic region is the freshwater engine of oceans around the globe. Melting Antarctic sea ice influences circulation thousands of kilometers away. Until 2016, the seasonal summer melt was triple the Amazon River’s entire annual flow of roughly 6,600 cubic km.

“From 2016, Antarctic sea ice shrank to record lows. This abruptly choked off that critical seasonal surge, and the meltwater delivery dropped to roughly double the Amazon’s annual flow.”

Co-author Professor Alberto Naveira Garabato, of the University of Southampton in the United Kingdom, described the changes as an urgent reminder that climate change is affecting almost every part of Earth’s surface.

“As this altered, saltier and denser water mass travels north, it moves across the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans. Because this water layer forms part of the upper limb of the ocean’s global ‘overturning circulation’, a sustained shift could, over years to decades, feed into the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation – the deep-ocean current system often linked to climate stability in the North Atlantic.

“It could also ultimately influence atmospheric circulation, weather, and storm tracks in the Southern Hemisphere. However, the impact can cascade globally.”

The globe shows sea ice around Antarctica month by month. The first time-series graph shows whether sea-ice area was above or below normal (the 1993-2024 mean), based on satellite observations. The bottom graph tracks the saltiness of Antarctic Intermediate Water, a layer that sinks from the surface into the ocean’s interior, using Argo float data from 2004. From 1993 to 2015, Antarctic sea ice slowly expanded (blue trend line), releasing more freshwater, making the waters beneath it fresher. After 2016, sea ice dropped sharply (red trend line), and the layer turned saltier. Less melting ice means less freshwater reaching the ocean interior. Credit: Kaushik Mishra

Changes in how water moves between the surface and deeper layers could also affect the oceans’ role as a “climate buffer,” as Gayen described it. Oceans absorb and redistribute most of the excess heat and a large share of human CO₂ emissions, storing them for decades to centuries. This slows and moderates atmospheric warming and its immediate effects.

Mishra said the abrupt reversal revealed a critical missing feedback loop.

“The ocean absorbs over 90 percent of all heat released into the environment by human activities, with most of that heat stored in the upper ocean. A weakened AAIW layer could push more excess heat deeper. That would mean existing models are underestimating deep-ocean warming and therefore miscalculating regional sea level rise and long-term ocean and land surface temperatures.”

“If the altered AAIW changes the way surface water is carried down into deeper layers, it could affect how much carbon the ocean locks away – although the magnitude and timing are uncertain,” Gayen said.

“This could be the tipping point for the Atlantic Ocean and the AAIW current, leading to larger, longer-lasting changes to the climate in the Southern Hemisphere.”

According to Gayen, the last time the AAIW switched was at the end of the last interglacial period, around 130,000 years ago, when there was very little ice in Antarctica.

“That transition took thousands of years, not two decades,” he said.

Reference: “Reversal of Antarctic Intermediate Water trends triggered by sea ice decline” by Kaushik Mishra, Bishakhdatta Gayen and Alberto C. Naveira Garabato, 28 October 2026, Nature Climate Change. DOI: 10.1038/s41558-026-02758-y

K.M. acknowledges the Prime Minister’s Research Fellowship (grant no. PMRF-0201843). B.G. acknowledges the Ministry of Earth Sciences Grant (grant no. MOES/11/2024) and the Australian Research Council Discovery Grant (grant no. DP240102823). A.C.N.G. acknowledges U.K. Research and Innovation guarantee funding for a European Research Council Advanced Grant (grant no. EP/X025136/1).

“Every Antarctic summer, melting sea ice sends a vast pulse of fresh water into the ocean.”

Inexplicably, the authors don’t mention why the melting sea ice is ‘fresh.’ Obviously, there is some snow on top of the ice. However, the main reason is that as sea water freezes, the dissolved salts are extruded from the crystal lattice of the forming ice, and cold, dense plums of concentrated brine sink into the depths. They have ignored half of the cycle and focused on the melting half, and implied that recent behavior portends a change in the long-term trend. Predictions are difficult when a system isn’t rigorously characterized and understood, which is the case with Antarctica. Antarctic shelf ice is is notoriously variable, and thus highly unpredictable. This is Chicken Little behavior of the wet feathers variety.

“That would mean existing models are underestimating deep-ocean warming and therefore miscalculating regional sea level rise and long-term ocean and land surface temperatures.”

Water is incompressible. Therefore, thermosteric expansion of the deep water by the speculated warming will be communicated to the sea level surface. Where is the evidence that this is happening?

#6511. Best Knife Set After Years of Testing Knives (2026)

I’m just going to say it: You don’t need an 18-piece knife block with a blade for every conceivable kitchen task. If you find one of those sets out in the wild, what you’ll probably find is that a lot of knives in the block still have a factory-sharp edge, because they’ve never been used. At the same time, it’s hard to ignore the sheer value a lot of knife sets offer. For most home cooks, buying every knife piecemeal is akin to adding a 15%–20% tax.

After testing dozens and dozens of knives and talking with our Test Kitchen editors and professional chefs, the consensus is that the best knife set really only needs three essentials: a chef’s knife, a bread knife, and a paring knife. As you get more confident or curious in the kitchen, you might choose to add a versatile nakiri knife, a handy petty knife, or a versatile cleaver, but we generally recommend doing so on an ad hoc basis with an eye for how it will fit into your cooking and how much you truly want to spend on a knife.

When it comes to the core pieces of a knife set, though, many of the best knife makers make great versions of multiple knife types. In that spirit, the sets here offer high performance and great value without compromise. Nearly every knife recommended in these sets has been tested individually, so I feel confident saying you’ll be happily slicing, sawing, and coring with every recommended option.

Read on for our top knife set picks, including a couple of slightly more expansive options with a knife block and steak knives for those who want some extra pieces.

New in this update: Editors spent some extended time with our top picks and we’ve added their long-term user notes.

Individual Mac knives have come out on top in our testing time and time again for their high-quality construction, ultrasharp blades, lightweight feel, and middle-of-the-road price point. This three-piece set is made up of a chef’s and petty knife that are the top overall picks in their respective categories, and a bread knife that’s essentially a luxe version of our favorite serrated knife.

In testing, the Mac Professional Chef’s Knife was versatile and comfortable to use thanks to its ergonomic pakkawood handle, able to work through a giant mound of veggies efficiently without making our hands cramp up. Its blade was one of the sharpest we tested and combines the best qualities of Japanese- and Western-style chef’s knives in both its material and shape. Made of molybdenum high carbon steel, it strikes a balance between the brittle (but extra-sharp) steel used in Japanese blades and the softer, more durable steel typical of a Western knife. Similarly, its shape is a hybrid of the rounded edge of a Western-style blade and the straighter edge of a Japanese knife.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, we are also big fans of Mac’s Professional Series petty knife, and for similar reasons: It’s razor-sharp and offers a unique shape that splits the difference between a utility knife and paring knife.

The bread knife included in this set is also part of Mac’s Professional Series. It’s a tier up from the Superior Series knife that won our bread knife test, which is evident in its build quality: While it features the same scalloped blade of the Superior Series knife, it has a metal bolster that makes for a more seamless connection between the blade and handle, and a more balanced overall feel while slicing.

In the long run: I used these Mac knives for more than a year (the chef’s knife I used for five) and they served me well the whole time. The paring knife is on the long side so it’s better suited to things like cutting hard cheeses than peeling or coring, though I prefer using a Y-peeler and an apple corer anyway. But because it’s longer, it was also easier to sharpen. The bread knife is perfect. The shape of the serrations and curve of the blade provide excellent leverage, and because they’re wavy instead of pointy, I didn’t notice loss of sharpness at all. It’s also heavy enough that its weight helps me push through without tearing.

And then there is the chef’s knife. The old standby, loved by every reviewer and Test Kitchen editor who has tried it. The balance, weight, and shape made it versatile, and the steel sharpened fantastically. However, after a couple years, my Mac did chip. I was able to resharpen and salvage it, but I’m not the only one who ended up with a chipped blade. The Mac we kept in house for long term testing also chipped after a few years. As reviewer Jesse Raub has noted in a number of his knife pieces, Japanese knives like the Mac are made from harder steel, so they don’t dull easily but they do chip. Personally, I find it one of those trade-offs you have to make when you’re picking a knife, and there is much good about the Mac that I still happily endorse it.

If you like the high-end look of beautiful Damascus steel and prefer a more rounded belly to your chef’s knife (better for rocking chops on the board), this set from Shun may be the one for you. Shun’s knives consistently perform well in our testing, and each of these knives has earned a spot as a top pick in its category. And by buying them as a set, you’ll save a modest amount of money off the total cost of the individual knives.

One of the things that sets Shun’s Classic line apart is that it features the brand’s proprietary VG-MAX core, a high carbon steel with additional metals like chromium and molybdenum added in the mix to help with corrosion resistance and sharpness. In testing, we found this made for blades that cut effortlessly through anything we threw at them and retained their sharpness over time.

The rounded pakkawood handles of the Classic line knives made each of them extremely comfortable to hold, and because the handles maintain an even thickness throughout their length, they allow each user to find the grip and hand positioning that’s best for them.

Shun’s knives are routinely some of the sharpest in our testing, and we appreciate the more Western-leaning hybrid shape of their blades. It makes them great options for anyone who wants the versatility of a Western chef’s knife while looking for the precision edge of Japanese gyuto. While Shun’s bread knife is a little short for our tastes, it was also the sharpest and easily sliced through everything during its round of testing, earning it a top pick in that category.

In the long run: I’ve had these Shun knives for a year now, and they’re my go-to set. The chef’s knife is incredibly comfortable to hold. A smooth notch where the blade meets the handle gives me a comfortable spot to pinch-grip, and the handle fits my small hands. The blade’s shape lets me glide and rock through tough ingredients. The paring knife is sharp and precise enough to hull strawberries but sturdy enough to cut into a thick wedge of Manchego. At nine inches, the bread knife handles most sourdough miches with ease, though I occasionally wish it were a little longer for really wide ones.

Renaissance 5-Piece Knife Set With Magnetic Board

Spending $400 on a knife set, like the Mac and Shun options above, is a big investment, even if you’re getting three high-quality blades. For a more budget-friendly alternative, we recommend this four-knife set (it gets called a five-piece set because the knife board counts as a piece) from Mercer Culinary’s Renaissance line. It’s a great cheap option for anyone who wants reliable knives without committing to a premium price point.

Mercer’s knives have consistently performed well in our testing, from the Renaissance line to the more affordable Genesis and Millennia collections. Their Millennia 10-inch Wavy Edge Bread Knife, priced under $16 when bought on its own, is even one of our top picks. In our tests, the Mercer chef’s, bread, and paring knives all delivered clean, consistent cuts and maintained their edges well after repeated use. While they didn’t outperform our favorite pricier knives, they came surprisingly close considering they were less than half the cost. Made from high carbon steel with full-tang construction and durable handles, the knives in this Renaissance set feel solid, well-balanced, and easy to control.

While we prefer the Japanese petty knife over a Western utility knife shape, there’s enough value in the core three knives of this set that we think it’s worth it for anyone who wants an affordable refresh or is stocking their kitchen for the first time.

In our testing for the best chef’s knives, Hedley & Bennett’s chef’s knife stood out as well-balanced, comfortable to grip, and easy to maneuver thanks to the seamless transition between the handle and blade. After months of use, our Test Kitchen editors were impressed with how well it held up. And while testers preferred the Mac, if you’re looking to bring some fun color into your kitchen while still investing in a high-performing knife set, Hedley & Bennett is a great choice.

This set includes a utility knife rather than a paring knife. It’s about two inches longer than a traditional paring knife (5.6 inches versus 3.5), making it a bit more versatile for larger tasks, such as slicing an oversized apple.

The bread knife is on the shorter side, at only 8.6 inches, but its sharp, tapered serrated edge allows for more controlled, precise cuts than some straight-blade designs. Deputy Food Editor Hana Asbrink notes that the blade’s slope also helps prevent your knuckles from hitting the cutting board, a common issue with bread knives that maintain the same width along the entire blade.

While they aren’t the sharpest knives out of the box, they’re made of high carbon stainless steel and can be easily sharpened to a finer edge. While we think most home cooks would like this set, its biggest advantage is the variety of colorways, which make for a more aesthetically pleasing kitchen.

In the long run: I’m in a less-is-more phase of my life, mostly because my shoe box of a kitchen leaves little room for 10 knives. So the pared down three from Hedley & Bennett fits perfectly in my space. They’re lightweight and the tapered spines have contributed to a welcome feeling of precision when using them. The chef’s knife gets the most use—there’s something rhythmic about slicing garlic with it. But the utility knife has come in handy more often than I thought. I’ve used it, along with my trusty kitchen shears, to break down whole chickens. And the angled tip of the serrated knife has made it useful for more than sawing through crusty bread. The blade shape helps for more delicate work like piercing tomato skin without mangling it.

With use, a few minor scuffs and scratches have started to show. My colleagues have also warned me that the handles can crack over time, though that hasn’t been an issue for me over the first several months. Bless the greater knife powers that be. I do make a point of never leaving my knives in the sink and always drying them thoroughly after washing.

—Nina Moskowitz, associate cooking editor

The Wüsthof Classic line helped define high-end knives both at home and in professional kitchens for decades. Over the years, Wüsthof Classic set the standard for what to expect for performance and durability—full-tang construction, high carbon stainless steel, and a razor-sharp edge that’s easy to maintain. In our tests, Wüsthof’s 8" chef’s knife has been a standout for many years, and the included bread knife and paring knife are also great options.

The big catch is that many cooks prefer the more nimble Japanese-style and hybrid knives, and Wüsthof’s heritage puts its Classic line in a more expensive bracket. Still, if you prefer the heft and durability of Western-style knife set, it’s hard to go wrong with this one—and they’ll last a lifetime with good upkeep.

If you’re looking for a more expansive knife set beyond our essential three-piece recommendation, Shun’s Classic line stands out. This seven-piece set includes the core trio—a chef’s knife, paring knife, and bread knife—plus two smart additions: a 6-inch petty knife and a pair of herb shears. The petty knife fills that sweet spot between a paring and a chef’s knife, perfect for tasks that need more precision than a big blade allows but would overwhelm a smaller one, like slicing citrus or trimming proteins.

The herb shears are a surprisingly handy upgrade. Instead of dragging out a cutting board just to mince some parsley or chives, you can snip them straight into a salad, soup, or garnish. Still, this is a good example of where a large set can sell you short: herb shears are less versatile than a standard set of heavy-duty kitchen shears.

The set also comes with a honing steel to keep your knives sharp and a sleek 11-slot bamboo storage block, which gives you extra space to add other styles down the line, like a nakiri for vegetable prep, a santoku, or even a cleaver.

In the long run: By jumping up to the larger seven-piece set I got to add my favorite part of the set: the herb scissors. I use them to snip parsley right over a finished dish without pulling out a cutting board. They’re small, but they can still cut raw chicken into chunks when I don’t feel like reaching for a knife. Just be sure to hand-wash and towel-dry them right away. If you leave them dripping wet, they will get watermarks.

Large knife sets that come with a storage block are handy—it’s literally a one-stop shop. And if you’re a fan of serving grilled ribeyes whole to your guests, you’re going to need some sharp steak knives. Global’s knives are strong performers in our tests, and their unibody construction makes them easy to clean and maintain. We also like their unique steel, which retains sharpness without being as brittle as other alloys.

While they can be polarizing, many people find their dimpled steel handles comfortable to hold, and their knives come sharp out of the box. A big reason we like this large set over other options is that larger knife sets are usually extremely expensive, or they’re made up of a knife maker's budget line. Here you see strong value for great knives, and the inclusion of a petty knife, a chef’s knife, and a kiritsuke-style slicing knife means there’s nothing you won’t be able to cut with swiftness and precision.

Given its size, it’s a well-balanced set, and the inclusion of the serrated utility knife is a nice touch for slicing tomatoes or peeling squash. It may feel like a hefty sticker price, but you’d be hard-pressed to find this many high-quality knives at this price point from other brands.

In the long run: While the Shun knives are my home set, the Global Chef’s knife is the one I always use when I’m working in the Test Kitchen. The balance and the size of the knives in this set (a slightly shorter chef’s and bread knives) are perfect for smaller women. Other BA editors have echoed this idea in the past. The secret is in the handle. Its dimpled steel gives you a secure grip, and it starts wide before tapering in, which makes it perfect for small hands. It feels hefty (it’s full of sand) while still being lightweight, which matters when you need to stay nimble with your knife cuts.

We’ve been testing knives for years now, and we have found that the same brands tend to come out on top across each knife category. Luckily for you, aspiring knife set purchasers, that means we’ve had no trouble finding three-piece sets from brands we know and love that feature product-test-winning, quality knives our team of experts can vouch for. Each set listed above is made up of individual knives we’ve tested against a long list of competitors and wholeheartedly approve of.

Head over to our individual reviews of the best chef’s knives, best bread knives, and best paring knives for even more information.

How many knives do you need in a knife set?

We firmly believe that three knives are all you really need: a chef’s knife, a paring knife, and a bread knife. Together, they cover just about every essential kitchen task, from chopping vegetables to slicing crusty loaves.

That said, if you’re looking to upgrade or expand your collection, three additional knives are excellent additions: a nakiri knife, a petty knife, and a cleaver. While not essential, they’re nice to have: the nakiri offers extra precision for vegetable prep, the petty knife is ideal for those in-between tasks that a paring or chef’s knife might not handle quite as neatly, and a cleaver can help tackle larger chopping tasks (or precision cuts with a Chinese cleaver).

Mac has come out on top of our knife testing across the three core knives—chef’s, serrated, and paring—but the question itself is sort of like asking “who is the best guitar player.” Different people will find different knife shapes, weights, and handle styles better or worse for their hands. And, there are a lot of small elite knife makers out there that make items that aren’t just kitchen tools, but works of art. If you want to investigate some of those, we’d encourage you to check out a shop like Chubo Knives for elite Japanese blades.

But as far as affordable, widely available knives go, Mac’s routinely outperformed the competition. They are made in Japan from molybdenum high carbon steel, which blends the durability of Western-style steel with the precision sharpness of traditional Japanese blades. The result is a knife that’s lightweight, versatile, and sharp. Mac’s bread knife took the top spot in our testing thanks to its 10.5-inch blade, which is an inch and a half longer than most. That extra length makes it easier to slice through wide loaves like focaccia in a single stroke.

We stand by all of our recommended knives, but what you will get if you buy higher-end knives are blades made from better steel that are finished with more care. That means they’ll hold an edge longer, require less sharpening, and last for years with proper care. For most home cooks, it’s worth investing at least $150–$200 in a chef’s knife since it’s the blade you’ll reach for every day. Secondary knives like paring, bread, or utility knives don’t need to be as pricey, but if you use them often, it may be worth upgrading those too (and getting them as part of a bundle in a small knife set is a good way to do that).

Read more here about how much you should spend on a knife.

Is it better to buy knives individually or as a set?

It depends on your priorities. The great part about a knife set is that it’s a one-and-done purchase. You get the three essentials (chef’s, bread, and paring knives), and you can trust that each knife in the set has been tested to perform at a high level. That said, buying individually gives you more flexibility. Maybe you prefer a 6-inch chef’s knife over an 8-inch or a longer bread knife like Mac’s 10.5-inch version over Shun’s 9-inch or Hedley & Bennett’s 8.6-inch tapered blade. Think of a set as a strong starting point: It gets you well-equipped right away, but you can always mix and match later as you learn what sizes and styles feel best in your hand.

In general, yes—most manufacturers will offer at least some discount when you buy knives as a set rather than one at a time. How much of a discount? Well, that varies. For some brands, buying a three-piece set is like getting a third knife for free. For others, you might only save a few bucks. Still, many sets will also go on sale, adding even more savings to the already discounted knives. At the end of the day, it’s worth pricing out each knife in a set to see how much you’ll save by buying the bundle, and weigh that against being able to pick your favorite knife from each type. Still, we find that if you’re a fan of one knife from a brand, you’ll probably enjoy the handle style and comfort of other knives from the same brand—combined with some savings, you get a strong argument for picking out a knife set when you need a kitchen refresh.

What’s the best way to store your knives?

Proper storage is just as important as proper sharpening when it comes to keeping your knives in good shape. No knife should ever be tossed into a drawer with other utensils—that’s a quick way to dull the edge, damage the blade, or worse, hurt someone.

The best storage option depends on your kitchen setup and preferences, but our favorite is a magnetic strip mounted on the wall. It keeps blades accessible, protects the edge, and works for all shapes and sizes, whether you’ve got a slim paring knife, a hefty cleaver, or even kitchen shears. Another big plus: magnetic strips take up zero counter or drawer space and are easy to clean with a quick wipe. These are our favorite magnetic strips.

Jesse Raub: I’ve been a professional kitchen product tester since 2021, where I tested nearly everything: espresso machines, wooden spoons, bread proofing baskets, pizza stones, garlic presses, and more. My fascination with kitchen knives began in 2003 when the chef at the kitchen where I worked let me use his personal Wüsthof knives during prep work one day. Over the last two years, I’ve tested over 70 different knives for Bon Appétit and written about the best knife sharpeners and how to best sharpen your knives at home. If you’re ever on the phone with me and hear a light scraping noise in the background, just know that I’m likely touching up my kitchen knives on a whetstone and testing their sharpness by slicing sheets of paper.

Additional testing by Olivia Tarantino and Noah Kaufman

#6510. Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in New York City

The akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit. It is a small but enduring presence, tended to around the clock, its care passed from one person to the next so that the light never goes out. I’ve often thought about how much of life is like this, how we are constantly passing the torch from one version of ourselves to another.

As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood. I was becoming someone different from the girl I had been, carrying parts of her with me but beginning to understand the world through a new lens. Now, years later, I find myself at another such transition: I am becoming a different version of a woman, one I am still getting to know.

In many ways, this transition is happening outside of me. Thirteen years ago, I moved away from my family in Mumbai and the home where Diwali had always been celebrated. For all those years, the rituals continued, even as I participated in them from thousands of miles away, mostly over video calls. Back in Mumbai, Diwali meant a house full of family and friends, kitchens bustling with cooking and frying, and the warm glow of diyas illuminating the mandir. I was no longer physically there, but I remained part of it. This year, for the first time, I hosted my parents for Diwali in the home I’ve built for myself in New York City.

It felt cataclysmic, or at least I was making it feel that way in my head. As I welcomed a different version of myself, I was also taking on a new role within my family. I was no longer simply the daughter returning to their house for Diwali; I was the one opening my home, preparing the food, tending to the rituals, and making space for the people who first taught me what this celebration means. There is perhaps no greater joy than watching the people I love receive and experience care. And yet, this was a responsibility I had chosen to take on, and one that felt particularly daunting as the eldest daughter. I wanted to get it right.

For me, that care has always found its way to the table. Food is how my family celebrates, how we mark occasions, and, perhaps most importantly, how we look after one another. So naturally, much of my energy went into planning the meal. Despite my best efforts, my dad promptly assigned himself the task of making the goat kari—apparently, even after 13 years away, some things hadn’t changed. We headed to our local butcher in Brooklyn to buy fresh goat meat, and almost immediately, his attention turned to the spice tolerance of my guests.

“How much spice can your friends tolerate?” he kept asking me. “Should I keep it at a level six? But our level six might be their level ten. What do I do?” he lamented. “Relax, they’ll be able to handle it! Just make it our level five,” I told him.

I gave in and handed over part of the kitchen to my mother, too. She took charge of the paneer, cooking generous chunks in a luscious onion-tomato gravy and making the chapatis. Selfishly, I didn’t mind relinquishing that responsibility: This would be my one chance for the year to eat chapatis fresh off the tava, puffed up and piping hot, and made by my mother.

As the days drew closer, I found myself loosening my grip on the plans I’d made. My parents had their own ideas about what needed to be cooked, and while I was initially resistant to them taking over (any immigrant will tell you how hard it is to get our parents to just relax!), I was learning that hosting didn’t necessarily mean doing everything myself. It also meant making room for everyone to contribute and allowing new rituals to form.

The evening began with freshly fried moong vadas. My mother, of course, insisted on frying them for everyone, right before serving. Made from soaked and ground mung lentils, these little fritters are crisp and golden on the outside, with a soft, almost creamy interior. They have a naturally earthy, nutty flavor from the lentils, sharpened with green chiles, ginger, and spices.

Moong vadas are best eaten immediately, still hot out of the oil, with a tangy green chutney. The scene reminded me of Diwalis back in Mumbai, when the vadas rarely even made it to the serving platter: Everyone would gather around the kitchen, waiting for the next batch to come out of the kadai, reaching for them before they had a chance to cool. I saw the same thing happening in my kitchen in New York.

In the meantime, my friends Leanne and Christina took charge of the tamarind margaritas, my ode to the soft, sweet-tart tamarind candies I grew up savoring as a kid. The tangy cocktails were a welcome counterpoint to the savory fritters, the perfect way to wake up our taste buds (and made exercising some restraint with those moong vadas before dinner particularly difficult). My brother helped set the table and move furniture around, just as we used to do for our parents back in Mumbai. There was something deeply comforting about watching us fall into these old rhythms.

The table eventually came together with a mix of dishes that felt both familiar and celebratory. There was chana masala from my cookbook, East to East, alongside my dad’s goat kari, slow-cooked with spices until the meat was tender. My mother’s saucy tomato-onion paneer was accompanied by a pile of chapatis that disappeared almost as quickly as they came off the stove. We served everything family-style, laying out the dishes on kansa thalis, traditional Indian plates made from bronze or bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. They reminded me of the way my grandparents served meals, and I wanted to bring a little of that into our Diwali celebration.

At the center of the spread was a vegetable pulao, fragrant basmati rice cooked with carrots, cabbage, cauliflower, and whole spices. Alongside it, I placed bowls of pickled onions and mango achaar, whose sharp, tangy bite cuts through the richness of the karis. There was also cucumber raita, cool and creamy, offering a welcome respite from the heat of the spices. These accompaniments might seem like small additions, but they are essential to the balance of an Indian meal. Every bite can be a little different, depending on what you bring together on your plate.

For dessert, I made homemade gulab jamun, my brother’s favorite. The soft dumplings are made from milk solids and fried until golden, then soaked in a warm saffron-and-cardamom-scented sugar syrup.

As I sat cuddled among both my families, I realized that while it wasn’t the perfectly orchestrated dinner I’d imagined when I first started planning, it was something better. The family I was born into celebrating Diwali alongside the family I’d chosen and built in New York, all gathered around the same table and enjoying every minute of it. Perhaps keeping the flame alive was never about re-creating the past exactly as it was but about allowing it to illuminate whatever comes next.

#6509. Brick Kilns Became Cleaner and More Profitable, but Workers Saw No Benefits

Bangladesh’s brick kilns found a way to pollute less and earn more, but workers saw no measurable improvement in their pay or working conditions.

Simple adjustments to how coal is fed and bricks are stacked helped traditional kilns burn less fuel, release less pollution, and produce better bricks. Yet a companion study found no measurable improvement in wages, health, child labor, or coercive working conditions during the study period.

The findings expose a gap between improving an industry’s performance and improving life for its workforce. They also suggest that protecting workers requires measures aimed directly at their needs.

The multiyear research effort involved Nina Brooks, an assistant professor at the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability and a faculty affiliate of its Center for South Asian Studies.

Bangladesh’s rapid urban growth depends on an industry with a substantial environmental footprint. The country is the world’s fourth-largest brick producer, and roughly 8,000 traditional kilns supply more than 90% of its domestic brick consumption. Alongside carbon emissions, the kilns release fine particles known as PM2.5. Ambient air pollution causes 4.9 million premature deaths globally, with South Asia accounting for 32% of them.

Brooks began investigating brickmaking about eight years ago during her doctoral studies. She and her collaborators mapped kilns with satellite imagery and machine learning, studied regulation, and examined health effects in communities downwind. Their work revealed why restricting kiln locations alone could not solve the pollution problem.

“Bangladesh is one of the world’s most densely populated countries,” Brooks said. “It is not feasible to move brick kilns away from all schools, health facilities, and urban centers that may be harmed by the pollution.”

Instead, researchers worked with owners, managers, and workers to improve existing operations. They introduced more continuous coal feeding, brick-stacking arrangements that improved airflow, and measures to reduce heat loss. None required replacing kilns or purchasing major new equipment.

After a small pilot, the team expanded the approach to hundreds of kilns. Results published in Science showed that training and technical support reduced energy use by about 10.5% across kilns assigned to the program. Estimated emissions fell by 171 metric tons (about 188.5 US tons) of carbon dioxide and 0.45 metric tons (about 990 pounds) of PM2.5 per kiln over a firing season.

Among kilns that adopted the practices because of the program, energy use dropped about 23%, while carbon dioxide and PM2.5 emissions each fell roughly 20%. Owners spent less on fuel and produced a greater proportion of higher-quality bricks.

Adoption had increased when researchers returned the next firing season, suggesting the changes had staying power. “Because the changes are economically beneficial for owners, they had a strong incentive to continue following them,” Brooks said.

For businesses facing expensive equipment upgrades and authorities struggling to enforce environmental rules, the findings offered a practical route to cleaner production.

The researchers then examined whether those business benefits reached workers. Bangladesh’s brick industry relies on a large, mostly informal workforce whose employment can involve debt, advance payments, long hours, hazardous conditions, and restrictions on leaving. A companion study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences examined 246 kilns in the Khulna Division and included private interviews with 1,442 workers.

Seventy percent of workers reported having no personal protective equipment, and 71% lacked a formal labor contract. Forty-two percent described restrictions on movement or communication. Across the sample, roughly 20% met the U.S. Department of State’s definitions of labor trafficking. At nearly half the kilns, at least 1 in 6 workers met those definitions.

Adult workers also reported child labor at more than 70% of the kilns, with most reported cases involving children ages 14 to 17.

The intervention lowered fuel costs by 9.6% and improved brick quality by 8.1%, but researchers detected no corresponding improvement in trafficking, child labor, wages, health, or working conditions. Although changes were possible within the study period, the economic gains did not produce measurable benefits for workers.

Higher productivity is often expected to help employees through better pay or conditions. The kiln studies show why that outcome cannot be assumed when coercion and limited bargaining power shape the labor market.

“In many countries, not just Bangladesh, labor laws are hard to enforce, particularly in informal sectors. So, it’s critical to find other ways to protect workers from exploitation,” said Grant Miller, a professor of medicine at Stanford University. “Our study shows that we cannot rely on productivity gains alone to do that, at least not in the short run. Finding approaches that work beyond regulation is a central goal of our ongoing research.”

Expanding the cleaner production program revealed that kiln owners in other regions were more reluctant to adopt the changes. In districts around Dhaka, owners were considerably less likely to adopt the practices than those in Khulna. Yet participating kilns achieved comparable reductions in fuel use and emissions, Brooks said. “So, we’re seeing greater hesitation,” she said. “But once they adopt, we see the same benefits.”

Sameer Maithel, the research team’s lead technical expert, said the reasons are still being investigated. Owners operating on narrow margins may hesitate to change familiar methods while facing unpredictable coal prices, brick demand, and regulation. Differences in kiln size, land, and production practices can also make adoption easier in one location than another.

“Informal brick production in South Asia faces a lot of uncertainty: weather, energy prices, market demand, and regulation all shift unpredictably. Many kiln owners also have limited technical and managerial support, and conditions vary from region to region,” Maithel said. “All of this makes scaling up slow and complex, and it takes sustained, dedicated effort.”

The lack of improvement for workers has prompted the team to test more direct measures. During the most recent brickmaking season, researchers returned to Khulna with recommendations developed through pilot work and conversations with workers.

They recommended masks for people crushing coal, goggles and protective footwear for fire workers, and head protection for brick carriers. Other measures included sanitation and cooking facilities, shaded rest areas, clean water, heat-stress awareness, and information about child labor.

“None of the owners I interviewed objected to improving conditions for workers, though some disagreed with specific components. They saw the cost as negligible compared to what they spend running a kiln. As they put it, if workers do better work because of it, it’s worth doing,” said Mohammad Saeed Munim, a research officer in the Health Systems and Population Studies Division of the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research in Bangladesh.

Researchers had expected more resistance. Owners’ willingness to consider these changes now gives the team an opportunity to test whether targeting workers’ daily needs can deliver improvements that greater productivity alone did not.

“Reducing emissions and air pollution from informal brick kilns: Evidence from Bangladesh” by Nina Brooks, Debashish Biswas, Sameer Maithel, Grant Miller, Aprajit Mahajan, M. Rofi Uddin, Shoeb Ahmed, Moogdho Mahzab, Mahbubur Rahman and Stephen P. Luby, 8 May 2025, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.adr7394

“Productivity gains and work conditions in coercive labor markets: Experimental evidence from the Bangladesh brick sector” by Grant Miller, Debashish Biswas, Aprajit Mahajan, Kimberly Singer Babiarz, Nina Brooks, Jessie Brunner, Sania Ashraf, Jack Shane, Alvise Scarabosio, Sameer Maithel, Shoeb Ahmed, Moogdho Mahzab, Mohammad Rofi Uddin, Mahbubur Rahman and Stephen P. Luby, 16 July 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2528388123

A stunning fossil owl from Germany that has its last meal preserved in its stomach helped researchers to narrow down the time when these birds mostly became active at night.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A fledgling owl that lived 47 million years ago in what is now Germany offers tantalizing new clues about when most of these birds became nocturnal, a new study shows. The discovery brings researchers one step closer to finally solving the biggest mystery about these birds.

The young owl is a newly described species named Masillastrix blattophaga. Researchers unearthed the almost perfectly preserved bird in 2025 in the Messel Pit, an ancient lake surrounded by a forest that is now the richest fossil site in the world for understanding life in the Eocene epoch (56 million to 34 million years ago). The skull is missing, but the rest of the fossil was so well preserved that researchers found the owl's last meal in its stomach: a greenish-blue, iridescent cockroach.

The cockroach is one of several pieces of evidence suggesting that this tiny owl was diurnal, or active primarily during the day. Iridescence is associated with a diurnal lifestyle, so it appears that the owl, which measured less than 5 inches (12 centimeters) long, was hunting in the daytime, researchers said in the new study.

This indicates that owls were not nocturnal 47 million years ago and so must have switched to the night-owl lifestyle more recently, said study first author Gerald Mayr, a paleontologist and head of ornithology at the Senckenberg Research Institute and the Natural History Museum Frankfurt in Germany.

"There exists a consensus that owls must have evolved from a diurnal ancestor," Mayr told Live Science in an email. That's because some early owl fossils have head-rotation structures similar to those of diurnal raptors and bony ridges above the eye sockets that could have shaded the owls' eyes from the sun.

Therefore, it is plausible that the Messel owl was fully diurnal, rather than active during the daytime and nighttime as some owls are today, because that would imply that some of its ancestors had already evolved nocturnal traits, Mayr said.

Researchers also found a cockroach identical to the one in the Messel owl's stomach in sediments just a few feet away from the new fossil. This well-preserved cockroach helped the team to identify the insect inside the owl, the researchers wrote in the study, which was published Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It's possible that the owl ate the cockroach at dawn or at dusk, which might cast doubt on whether the bird was diurnal. But there are other clues hinting that the owl was diurnal, including the appearance of some of the owl's feathers and the stoutness of its upper wing bones.

Mayr said he and his colleagues believe the shape of the upper wing bones, or humeri, is an indicator of when owls are active. The Messel owl's stocky humeri hint that the species flew during the day, when silent movement doesn't confer a significant advantage because there is enough light to see predators. Conversely, modern nocturnal owls have slim humeri and fly almost soundlessly, he said.

The fossil was so well preserved that researchers identified a cockroach in the stomach that was likely the owl's last meal.

Assuming this hypothesis is correct, the earliest known nocturnal owl species are from about 35 million years ago, in the Late Eocene, Mayr said. Owl fossils from this period and more recently look a lot like modern owls and have elongated humeri, he noted. The oldest known owl in the fossil record, Ogygoptynx wetmorei, dates to around 60 million years ago.

This means that owls likely became nocturnal between 47 million and 35 million years ago. This is the best current estimate, because the owl fossil record is very sparse and species are often described from only a few isolated bones, according to the study.

"We still know so little about the early evolution of modern birds," Mayr said, adding that every fossil discovery has the power to change even well-established ideas in the field.

The big question that remains is why owls became nocturnal. Previous theories suggested that owls evolved this behavior to avoid competition with diurnal birds of prey or to benefit from a proliferation of nocturnal mammals. But studies show that both of these groups exploded much later than 35 million years ago — around 20 million to 25 million years ago — suggesting there wasn't a clear advantage driving owls to switch to nocturnal lifestyles at that time.

The new results have deepened the uncertainty of why owls turned nocturnal. But "by narrowing down the time frame when owls became nocturnal, our study may eventually contribute to solving this mystery," Mayr said.

Mayr, G., Šmídová, L., Richter, A., & Wedmann, S. (2026). Evidence for diurnal habits in an exceptionally preserved Eocene owl. Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.09.079

Sascha is a U.K.-based staff writer at Live Science. She holds a bachelor’s degree in biology from the University of Southampton in England and a master’s degree in science communication from Imperial College London. Her work has appeared in The Guardian and the health website Zoe. Besides writing, she enjoys playing tennis, bread-making and browsing second-hand shops for hidden gems.

#6506. A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

On a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo. Six lanes of traffic jockeyed inches from her left shoulder, while the black waters of the Río Ozama coursed below. “Oh my God, Oli, what are we doing?” she said. “Nobody does this.” Evangelista is the communications manager for Santo Domingo’s most intriguing restaurant, Casarré. Her boss, Swiss Dominican chef Olivier Bur, was leading Evangelista, photographer Clay Williams, and me beyond the fortified walls of the Zona Colonial, where few travel on foot.

On the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge. Live bachata drowned out the traffic overhead. Bur procured a big bottle of Presidente and plastic cups from a vendor, poured, and raised a “Salud!”

Bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere. Moving slowly, he’s learned the textures of the city. Still, for the next six days, he took Williams and me to his most beloved restaurants by car. We visited a string of chimi stands where hawkers compete for clientele through the night; a chicharrón spot where couples dance shoeless on the cool tile floor; and a cafeteria where boys shuffle stewed eggplant, beets, and goat to bus drivers en route. Places like these are the “infrastructure for life,” Bur said. “Thirty years ago, there was nothing else.”

Over the last couple of decades, however, another dining scene has sprouted. Dominican chefs have returned from kitchens in Mexico, Japan, or Switzerland to explore the forgotten and sometimes shunned ingredients of their (or their parents’) homes. They served us conch, cassava, breadfruit, and djon-djon mushrooms in sashimis, foams, tostones, and surprising dessert creams. The dishes were fresh and exciting, but local and global traditions have always mingled—as such, the cuisine is not “New Dominican,” it’s simply “Dominican,” fully expressed.

Calle Andrés Julio Aybar 13+1 829 545 7503

The Piantini neighborhood was once verdant and sleepy, according to Bur. Now it’s a bustling business district. Most of the remaining vegetation decorates the façades of restaurants, like Ajualä’s. Brushed palm thatch and a bushy barba de Fidel (Fidel’s beard) tree greet you at the tall aged-steel door.

Venezuelan chef Saverio Stassi is a leader among the culinary new guard. His treatment of local ingredients is virtuosic. He confits guinea hen in cocoa butter and tops breadfruit tostones with local yellowfin and Cambita avocado; and over two days, his team bathes the succulent goat from the northwest—where they famously graze on wild oregano, self-infusing their meat—in Seville orange juice before roasting it in a barbacoa pit.

Calle Max Henríquez Ureña 14+1 809 547 3592

Chef Erik Malmsten has cooked at his parents’ cabaret in Gothenburg, Sweden, at Aquavit in New York, and at Bocuse d’Or competitions around the world. But to take his career to the next level, he returned to his mother’s homeland to open a Nordic-Japanese restaurant.

“You’ll see, it’s really good,” Bur told us. The meal starts with “lobster chicharrón,” with a reduced crustacean bisque, fried into airy orange sheets of bubbly crackling and served with tōgarashi Kewpie. Then, a parade of sashimi, like king fish, served with brown butter soy emulsion, ikura, and lemon zest. It ends with Dominican chocolates, molded, painted, and plated to look like koi fish on a synchronized swim.

If, like me, you come from a pizza region, you might not be inclined to use one of your Santo Domingo meal slots on a pie. But I urge you: Make time for Casa Gazcue. Spanish Dominican chef Francis Pena’s 48-hour-fermented crust comes blistered and sometimes covered in honeyed sesame seeds. Iterations are variously laden with spicy Dominican oxtail, chimi sandwich sauce, pistachio, and jamón ibérico, but you don’t have to choose: For groups, he serves a rosca (a round with an open middle) of six sections arranged like floral pizza petals.

In 1954, the Bonarelli family opened the legendary Italian restaurant Vesuvio. For decades, it was the place—the only place—to go out for a formal sit-down meal around here. Vesuvio closed over 20 years ago, but the founder’s grandson, Giancarlo Bonarelli, now runs Bottega Fratelli in a sleek modern building in Naco (Piantini’s equally upscale neighbor).

You’ll notice a great variety of beet dishes in the Dominican Republic. Farmers harvest them year-round in the cool, pine-forested Costanza Valley. Try them here, roasted and served with blue cheese, chèvre, candied nuts, and honey. Also try a carpaccio of king mackerel, caught off the eastern coast, or any of the risottos, an emblem of the family’s enduring Italian culinary influence.

Hideyoshi Tateyama’s parents opened Samurai in 1990. The restaurant joined Vesuvio, along with one or two others in that era’s small restaurant scene. It still stands out today among the many dozens.

Be sure to order the guatapaná con coco. A tried-and-true combo of shrimp and coconut imbued with native guatapaná leaf, tobiko, sesame seed, and scallion—it’s been on the menu for two decades. Also, don’t miss the chance to sample a sashimi of the meter-long “calamar diamante” from the Samaná region. It’s simply brightened with lemon zest. Meals are capped with a green tea amaro. Once a month, Tateyama personally runs a chef’s-choice omakase service.

On the day we visited Villar Hermanos, lines formed around the block for each of two buffets. Women balanced towers of takeout containers tightly wrapped in plastic. It was the World Cup Final, and people were rushing to get some of the city’s best comfort food to their coffee tables. “This is the place to come for all the Dominican classics,” Bur told us.

We found a large table under the sprawling canopy of a banyan tree and ordered mofongo. It was moist, punctuated with crisp chicharrón crackling. The sancocho, the classic Domincan stew thick with potato and yuca starch, assumed extra body when alternating spoonfuls of broth and rice. While I didn’t have my coveted mangú and tres golpes (salami, queso frito, and eggs), I would trade my house and car to live next door and eat breakfast there every morning under the filtered sun.

Avenida San Vicente de Paúl, Santo Domingo Este 11504+1 809 244 8906

On Avenida San Vicente de Paúl in East Santo Domingo, scooters zip down the busy street all through the night, many popping over a curb into the Plaza Del Chimi. The “plaza” is a stretch of  10 to 15 “chimi” sandwich stalls outfitted with griddles and prep stations heaped with roasted pork shoulders. Dealers quickly slice the meat, lay it on the griddle, flip it onto a squishy pan de agua roll, and top it with cabbage, tomato, and tangy pink sauce before sliding it into your mitts. The stalls are open till 6 a.m. When they run out of beer, a man runs bottles from a cooler at his house and serves them in paper bags.

Avenida Independencia KM 8+1 809 532 2580

Across from a shopping mall on Avenida Indepencia, about a dozen cars cram into five parking spaces for the lunch or late-night staple pica pollo. Behind a crowded serving station, a woman slides eight pounds of chicken into a hotel pan, and the picking begins. Six sets of tongs compete for room, like bird beaks, snapping the chicken into styrofoam containers before barely holding them shut with strained rubber bands. Another eight pounds comes out less than two minutes later.

Pica pollo is one of the lasting influences of Chinese immigrants in Santo Domingo. Usually cooks marinate it in bitter orange, garlic, and oregano before coating it in flour and spice (in this case we detected Chinese five-spice) and deep-frying it to golden brown.

At Parque Mirador Sur, teens and whole families perch along concrete walls and hilltops eating fried yuca and succulent mojo-dipped chicharrón with long toothpicks. It comes from the crowded, steel-barred serving window across the street: Chicharrones Light de la Cayetano.

Among all the chicharrón we ate in the city (there was a lot), theirs stood out. There’s a small covered seating area where you can order beer to share. Bachata plays loud over a hanging speaker. Women take turns kicking off their heels to do the four-step shimmy with their jevos (boyfriends).

The Colmado, Bur says, “is essential to Dominican life. Everything happens there.” For 70 years, Colmado La Venganza has anchored a prominent corner in the Don Bosco neighborhood. It’s hosted thousands of late-night domino games and sports viewing parties. We were there during the World Cup.

At the entrance, a man with a crisp-edged haircut, big sunglasses, and a pressed floral shirt parked his shoe on a milk crate while a boy polished it with a rag. Inside, groups spanning all ages gathered at high-tops and around the bar. Folks shared triple-stacked ham, pickle, and cheese sandwiches, pressed, cubed, and spiked with toothpicks: the “sándwich especial.” Leaving the bar, chef Raniel Cruz (part of our party) texted his mom in Montreal. She responded: “Wait, you’re at Venganza? I used to drink there.”

One couldn’t understand the Dominican Republic’s vast culinary splendor in a lifetime, but if you had just one night to try, you’d want to dine at Casarré. Every Tuesday, the team takes excursions. We accompanied them to meet the countryside cooks, who wrap guáyiga root masa in leaves from the almond trees on Najayo beach and bake it in coal-covered pots. We visited a produce market, where vendors passed fruit samples, like little red “frutas milagrosas” that, when chewed beforehand, make bitter limes taste like sweet limeade.

At night, in a candlelit, contemplative room in the Zona Colonial, Bur and his team showcase their findings in a series of sublime, thoughtful dishes. On our visit, they presented djon-djon mushrooms from the Haitian borderlands in a sweet, guáyiga-thickened foam and in the broth of a citrusy okra and fish soup. Chef Isabella Sánchez explained: “The broth is murky, like the current state of the Río Ozama. It represents the negative aspects of our water—contamination and conflict—and the beautiful: the fish, the beaches, and our grandmother’s tea.”

Smoke from an open Uruguayan-style parrilla floats in the soft light over two stories. Our waiter said, “We want this to feel like a Sunday asado.” Indeed, the smoke, the char, and the Malbec are there. This asado, though, also has Negronis smoked tableside and poured from a glass goose. As we awaited a perfect aged rib eye, we enjoyed paper-thin beef carpaccio with foie, and a paella-esque rice with soft leeks, cilantro, and pork trotters.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

#6505. A Common Plastic Could Solve a Major Problem With Living on the Moon

The same plastic that keeps marathon runners warm could help future moon bases withstand extreme temperatures and years of rough treatment.

Engineers at the University of Pennsylvania have developed an insulating material by stacking hundreds of thin sheets of Mylar. In laboratory tests, the stacks combined effective insulation in a vacuum with flexibility and resistance to repeated compression, qualities that could make them useful for long-term lunar construction.

Their study, published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, calls the material hybrid layered insulating film stacks (HyLIFS). The approach addresses a persistent engineering problem: materials that resist heat flow often struggle to withstand physical damage.

“These stacks of Mylar can bend, withstand substantial compression, and maintain their insulating performance,” says senior author Igor Bargatin, an associate professor in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics (MEAM), “potentially allowing them to be packed, transported, and survive rough treatment over many years of use.”

On the moon, insulation must protect against temperatures ranging from hundreds of degrees below zero to the boiling point of water. But surviving those extremes is only part of the job. Materials must also endure transportation, installation, maintenance, and accidental impacts.

Some leading insulators are poorly suited to that treatment. Aerogels contain mostly empty space, making them lightweight and effective at slowing heat transfer in applications from industrial pipelines to NASA’s Mars rovers. Their porous structure, however, can also leave them susceptible to mechanical damage.

Multilayer insulation, widely used in space, takes another approach: reflective sheets separated by insulating spacers reduce heat transfer by radiation. These assemblies work well thermally, but they are not built to carry substantial loads and can tear during handling.

Making an insulator stronger can compromise its thermal performance. “For lunar infrastructure, we would ideally like both,” says Bargatin. “The ideal material is both resistant to damage and to the loss of heat.”

Mylar offered the researchers an accessible starting material. Formally known as biaxially oriented polyethylene terephthalate, or BoPET, the plastic already appears in food packaging and aerospace equipment. Combined with aluminum, it reflects infrared radiation, which is how shiny emergency blankets help marathon runners retain body heat.

The team tested several film thicknesses and coated some sheets with an extremely thin layer of aluminum oxide, also called alumina, to increase stiffness. Researchers then assembled the films individually into stacks.

“At the moment, the process is very time-consuming,” says first author Danielle R. Levin, a recent Penn chemistry doctoral graduate who also earned a master’s in MEAM. “We use two pairs of tweezers and small weights to handle and stack the delicate films. Even breathing near the stack can send the layers flying.”

Once assembled, however, the films were far tougher than their delicate handling suggested. Under vacuum conditions and compression representative of a lunar habitat with indoor air at atmospheric pressure, the best stacks matched the thermal conductivity of other high-performance vacuum insulation technologies while remaining flexible.

In separate mechanical tests, the coated stacks retained their insulating performance at the highest compressive stresses the laboratory equipment could produce. Researchers repeatedly squeezed samples to approximately 20 megapascals (about 2,900 pounds per square inch), roughly equivalent to concentrating 200 pounds onto an area the size of a fingertip.

“We were concerned about the material failing under such high compressive stress,” recalls Levin. “But the stacks didn’t survive just one high-stress cycle—they survived 10 in a row.”

That durability could make the material easier to transport and reuse, as well as more forgiving once installed. “You could use these stacks to insulate a lunar habitation, but astronauts will inevitably have little accidents where they bump into them,” says Bargatin. “When we’re talking about long-term habitation on the moon, it’s really important to have tough materials that can last long enough.”

“The combination of thermal and mechanical robustness is critical for long-term use on the moon,” says Levin. “This material could open a pathway to inexpensive, durable, and reusable lunar insulation.”

The study also identified an overlooked feature of commercial Mylar that could help explain its performance: microscopic particles added to keep the plastic from sticking to itself. These “antiblocking” particles protrude slightly from the surface, separating neighboring sheets and making thin films easier to manufacture and handle.

Their industrial purpose was already understood, but their influence on heat flow through stacked films had received little attention, according to the researchers. Because conventional multilayer insulation primarily targets radiation, there had been less reason to investigate how these particles affect heat conducted directly between sheets.

The researchers built models of heat transfer across the interfaces between layers and compared their predictions with experimental measurements. The results suggest that, in a vacuum, heat passes between sheets mainly at the tiny contact points where antiblocking particles touch neighboring films.

Those contacts could become a design tool. Instead of working around whatever particles commercial Mylar happens to contain, future insulation could use carefully selected particle sizes, numbers, and distributions to regulate heat transfer.

The particles also helped explain a result that contradicted the team’s initial expectations. Thinner sheets should allow more layers to fit into a given space, creating more interfaces that impede heat transfer. The researchers therefore expected their thinnest films to provide the strongest insulation.

Instead, the thinnest films they successfully characterized performed similarly to medium-thickness films when both received an alumina coating. The team suspects that particles in the thinner films create additional contact between neighboring layers, opening more pathways for heat to flow.

“As you compress the layers, the contact landscape changes,” says Levin. “It’s not just a matter of minimizing the film thickness or the number of particles; we must also account for how the contacts change and the films deform as pressure increases.”

Improving the material will therefore require balancing film thickness, stiffness, and particle distribution. Simply making each sheet thinner may provide little benefit if the resulting contacts allow more heat through.

The current samples cover only about one square centimeter (0.16 square inches), and manually cutting and stacking them takes hours. Producing practical insulation at the scale of a meter (about 3.3 feet) will require a much faster assembly method.

The researchers see potential in manufacturing techniques such as continuously coating large rolls of Mylar. Eventually, film thickness, coatings, and particle distribution might be adjusted before the material is wound into large stacks.

Larger versions still need testing, including whether they can withstand repeated bending, bumps, and scuffs. If the laboratory results carry over to practical production, HyLIFS could provide flexible insulation for lunar habitats, spacesuits, rovers, electronics, and other equipment that must operate for years in space.

For Levin, the findings show how much remains to be discovered in familiar materials. “The simplest configuration ended up being the best one,” she says.

Reference: “Robust Layered Thermal Insulator Film Stacks for Vacuum Applications” by D. R. Levin, M. F. Campbell, G. Aldan, O. H. Omodior and I. Bargatin, 1 September 2026, ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces. DOI: 10.1021/acsami.6c09126

This work was supported by the National Science Foundation Division of Chemical, Bioengineering, Environmental and Transport Systems (grant number 1845933) and Penn Engineering.
