#6407. 9 NYC Christmas Markets for Food, Fun, and Getting All Your Gift Shopping Done

New York City is electric any time of year, but few months on the calendar are as magical as the final two. In the run up to Christmas in New York, the Big Apple transforms into a holiday winter wonderland: think twinkling lights on street posts, elaborate department store window displays, and marquee theater events like New York City Ballet’s The Nutcracker or the Radio City Rockettes. It’s also probably the best time of the year to shop, thanks to a flurry of NYC Christmas markets that set up everywhere from Bryant Park to Grand Central Terminal.

But with so many to choose from, and locations all over the boroughs, how do you know which one is best for you to visit? That’s where we come in. Not only are we yearly visitors to all the annual markets, we’ve already done the research to scout the best newcomers to the field for 2026. Below, find our New Yorker-vetted NYC Christmas markets worth a holiday visit, from favorite and famed ones like Union Square’s, to newer events like Eater Under Wraps and Field + Supply.

Read our complete New York City travel guide here, which includes:

The rink at Bryant Park is tied only with Wollman in Central Park for the title of most famous in the city, and it's part of the Winter Village that runs here every year.

Location: Bryant Park, New York, NY 10018

Why we love it: There’s something for everyone at the massive Bank of America Winter Village at Bryant Park in the heart of Midtown. Gift givers will love The Holiday Shops by Urbanspace, a European-style market made up of “jewel box” kiosks filled with 180-plus vendors stocking everything from cozy winter hats to artisanal ornaments, while outdoor food stands at The Lodge provide plenty of fuel like s’mores and sausages for your shopping escapades. The Winter Village is also home to one of the city’s most famed ice rinks, which is free to use (though skate rental fees apply if you don’t bring your own).

The Grand Central Holiday Fair is celebrating its 21st year within the iconic terminal's shuttle passage.

Location: Vanderbilt Hall, Grand Central Terminal, 89 E. 42nd Street, New York, NY 10017

Why we love it: If you’re not exactly a fan of the cold weather, we have good news: New York City is also home to a handful of fantastic indoor holiday markets. The longest-running is the Grand Central Holiday Fair inside the city’s transportation crown jewel, Grand Central Terminal. The train station’s annual Holiday Fair inside Vanderbilt Hall features over thirty small businesses selling handmade gifts, plus an Uncommon Goods pop-up and an outpost of the Grand Central Gift Shop for all the train lovers on your list. And speaking of trains: after you’re done shopping, stick around the Terminal to watch the famed Holiday Train Show, featuring model trains trundling along decorated tracks that feature NYC landmarks and even the North Pole.

Union Square Holiday Market remains the gold standard classic for most New Yorkers, with 185 vendors spiraling out in a seemingly endless array of booths.

Location: Union Square, New York, NY 10003

Why we love it: If you say “holiday market” to a New Yorker, chances are they’ll direct you to the bustling Union Square Holiday Market. With nearly 200 vendors spread across concentric half-circles of booths, we’re not exaggerating when we say you can find the perfect present for everyone on your list at this sprawling pop-up. Some buzzy vendors to look out for this year? The MB Edit for vintage accessories and silk scarves, Hudson Valley Seed Company for organic bulbs and seeds, and make sure to save time to explore the many food purveyors for snacks, like Fan-Fan Donuts from James Beard Award nominee Fany Gerson. Pro tip: As the city’s most famous market, it can get quite crowded on nights and weekends, so try to opt for daytime weekday visits if possible.

Location: 100 W. 77th Street, New York, NY 10024

Dates: Every Sunday from November 29 until December 30 (and Saturdays December 12 and December 19)

Why we love it: While many of New York’s most famed holiday markets have the polish so closely associated with the city, one of the reasons Grand Holiday Bazaar is beloved is that it feels like a proper neighborhood event. Held every Sunday in a combo indoor-outdoor space on the Upper West Side, the Bazaar hosts over 150 independent, rotating local vendors who sell everything from handmade holiday decor to vintage accessories to skincare. Plus, 100 percent of the event’s profits are donated to four local public schools that serve over 2,000 kids.

FAD Market Holiday Pop-Up will set up shop in the lobby of Empire Stores in Dumbo, also home to Time Out Market.

Location: Empire Stores, 55 Water Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201 (Dumbo) and St. Paul, 190 Court Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201 (Cobble Hill)

Dates: November 30 – December 20 (Dumbo) and December 5–6, 12–13, and 19–20 (Cobble Hill)

Why we love it: FAD (which stands for Fashion, Art, Design) will host double the markets this year, in two separate locations in Brooklyn. Dumbo, which will run continuously from November 30th until December 20th inside Empire Stores, will have a rotating selection of jewelry makers, ceramicists, and small-batch food purveyors, with about 35 vendors on weekends and 14 during the week. Cobble Hill’s pop-up, meanwhile, will run over three weekends in December at St. Paul church, with a brand-new crew of 70-plus makers selling giftables like apparel, home decor, and skincare.

Turkish jewelry, fondue baguettes, and artisan soaps are on offer at Columbus Circle's Central Park-adjacent Christmas market.

Location: Columbus Circle, New York, NY, 10019

Why we love it: Situated at one of the prettiest corners of Manhattan—smack between Columbus Circle and Central Park—this market would be worth the trip even if the vendors were hawking only touristy souvenirs. Luckily though, the selection here is carefully curated, with makers this year ranging from Seyahan’s Turkish-inspired jewelry to Fairy Greens Lavender Farm’s fragrant collection of candles, soaps, and body oils made with the dreamy plant. There’s also plenty to snack on: don’t miss first-time vendor Fondue Baguette selling—you guessed it—baguettes filled with cheese.

Location: Herald Square, New York, NY 10001

Field + Supply, one of upstate New York's premier makers' markets, has landed in the city for the first time this year with a weekend pop-up in the Starrett-Lehigh Building.

Location: Starrett-Lehigh Building, 601 W. 26th Street, New York, NY 10001

Why we love it: One of upstate New York’s premier makers’ markets returns to the city this year, much to the delight of anyone looking for chic home goods, artisanal jewelry, and much more. There will be 140-plus vendors at the two-day Field + Supply event in Chelsea, with products ranging from ceramics to textiles to specialty foods. And even if you’re shopped out, there’s plenty else to lure you, including a visit from Santa himself and retro tintype portraits.

Location: Iron23, 29 W. 23rd Street, New York, NY 10010

Why we love it: The ultimate one-stop-shop for foodies, Eater Under Wraps, returns for a one-day-only market this year in Chelsea. Brands like Pepsi, Reese’s, and Kahlúa will host activations, along with food and drink samples from local spots like Shania's Max Bet and Nishaan, and, naturally, a robust, curated selection of gifts chosen by Eater’s own editors.

#6406. Flowers with clear petal ‘windows’ carry fewer microbes, which influences pollinators

Clear petal windows let infrared heat into two Florida shrubs' blooms, and warmth, not ultraviolet, thins out the flower microbes inside.

Some flowers have tiny, clear windows built right into their petals. While they might just look like a pretty design, researchers at Florida Atlantic University (FAU) have discovered that these see-through spots actually control the temperature inside the flower, changing the nectar and affecting how insects pollinate them.

Ultraviolet is the part of sunlight known for killing microbes, so the windows looked like a way of letting the sun scrub a flower clean.

Instead, the heat-carrying infrared coming through them is what mattered: warmer flowers held fewer microbes, and the ultraviolet didn’t explain the difference.

Jessica Williams, a Ph.D. student at Florida Atlantic University, did the work with four colleagues. They focused on shrubs named Lyonia lucida (also called fetterbush), and Lyonia fruticosa.

They are close relatives in the heath family that also includes blueberries. Both grow in the sandy, sun-baked scrub of south-central Florida and bloom together in late spring.

Each flower is a narrow urn with its petals fused into a chamber, and near the base of that urn a patch of petal has almost no pigment in it.

Other members of the family have the same windows, blueberries among them, and Williams’ team asked what they do to the light and heat inside.

Fetterbush flowers are visited mostly by moths at night, while L. fruticosa gets bees and wasps. Those visitors are probably how most microbes reach a flower.

Over three days in May 2025 at Archbold Biological Station, the team took seven flowers from each of nine plants per species, 126 in all.

For every flower, a thin temperature probe went in through the opening to the base of the chamber while a second probe hung just outside the petals.

Then the flower was clipped off with sterile scissors, dropped into a tube and kept on ice. Within five hours it was rinsed with a few drops of sterile water, pumped in and out five times.

That rinse went onto growth plates for two days at 81°F (27°C), and the team counted the colonies of yeast, mold and bacteria that grew.

Across the 108 flowers with a full set of measurements, the warmer a flower was inside, the fewer microbes grew from its rinse. Yeasts were the most common, then molds, then bacteria, and in both species the warmer flowers had fewer yeasts.

The two shrubs didn’t respond the same way. In L. fruticosa, warmer flowers had fewer bacteria, while in fetterbush the temperature made little difference to the bacteria. Fetterbush also carried more mold.

A fetterbush flower warmed by a bit more than half a degree for every degree the air around it warmed. An L. fruticosa flower barely moved, staying warmer than the air when the air was cool and cooler than the air when it was hot.

So a microbe’s experience of a hot May day depends on which shrub it landed in.

Heat was already known to matter to these microbes. A 2022 study in Frontiers in Microbiology found that heat can change which bacteria live in a flower’s nectar.

The windows let through more light than the pigmented petal, both ultraviolet and infrared. So the team tested the obvious idea, that ultraviolet was sterilizing the flower.

A germicidal ultraviolet lamp did kill. After 30 seconds under it, the share of L. fruticosa rinses with any yeast fell from 90 to 60 percent.

But microbes from flowers whose windows let through more ultraviolet were no better at surviving the lamp than microbes from flowers that let through less. The lamp was probably harsher than the ultraviolet a flower typically sees inside, Williams’ team wrote.

Infrared was a different story. In May 2026 the team chilled cut flowers in a refrigerator, then set them under a 500-watt halogen work light behind a filter.

One filter passed only deep red and infrared, and the other blocked infrared and passed only visible light. A probe inside each flower logged its temperature for 10 minutes.

Fetterbush flowers under infrared alone warmed about 5.8°F (3.21°C) more than flowers with the infrared blocked. After 10 minutes, they were 12.9°F (7.18°C) above where they started.

L. fruticosa flowers warmed about the same amount under either filter. Infrared, in other words, does warm a fetterbush flower.

Williams’ team doesn’t claim the windows evolved to keep microbes out. The chain they describe runs the other way. The windows let infrared in and, in fetterbush at least, the infrared warms the flower.

The warmth then probably makes the flower a harder place for microbes to persist. Microbes were still present in warm flowers, only fewer of them.

The windows may be doing several other jobs at once, the team wrote. Those could run from helping pollen develop to changing how bright the inside of the flower looks to a visiting insect. Fewer microbes would then be a side effect of those jobs.

“One of the exciting things about this work is that a seemingly small floral trait can change the physical environment inside a flower in ways that affect its microbial community,” Williams said.

“Because floral microbes can influence nectar traits and plant-pollinator interactions, these results suggest that flower structure may have ecological consequences that extend beyond the flower itself.”

Nectar and pollinators were not measured here. The field sampling covered 18 plants at one station over three days, and growth plates count only the microbes that will grow in a lab dish.

The team measured heat, not who delivered the microbes. Moths and bees bring different passengers, and which ones arrive first and how they compete inside the flower also shape which microbes settle in.

How those arrivals interact with the heat is, in the team’s words, an open question.

A warmer flower may also keep a different set of microbes rather than simply fewer, a subset that can take the heat. The study didn’t test that.

Finding out would mean identifying which microbes each kind of visitor drops off and which of them survive a warm afternoon inside a fetterbush flower.

The full study was published in the journal New Phytologist.

This tiny inkwell contains an alphabetic inscription in ancient Etruscan, a language that has never been fully decoded.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The chicken-shaped, black-glazed vase has an abecedarium ‪—‬ an inscription with the 26 letters of the Etruscan alphabet in order.

What it is: A bird-shaped ceramic inkwell

This small terra-cotta vase, which is shaped like a cockerel or young male chicken with human feet, was discovered in central Italy and was made by the ancient Etruscans. The potter inscribed the Etruscan alphabet on the body of the chicken, giving modern researchers clues to a language that has never been fully deciphered.

The vase stands just over 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. The dark-black ceramic, known as bucchero, was made through a unique firing method that prevented the kiln from getting enough oxygen, which caused the clay to absorb carbon. Bucchero is considered the trademark Etruscan ceramic, and it was produced from the seventh to the fourth centuries B.C. by this pre-Roman society. It is unclear where the cockerel vase was originally found, but it may have been discovered in a grave in one of the many cemeteries that surround Viterbo, which was originally an Etruscan town about 50 miles (80 kilometers) northwest of modern-day Rome.

According to The Met, the vase may have been a portable inkwell used by an ancient Etruscan who was learning how to write. The cockerel's head was the stopper, and it was loosely attached to the body by a cord through a set of loops. The inscription on the body of the vase is known as an abecedarium ‪—‬ the sequential list of letters in an alphabet.

The Etruscan alphabet is well known, since it was adopted from a regional version of the Greek alphabet in the early eighth century B.C. There were 26 letters in the Etruscan alphabet, but one of them in this abecedarium is incorrect. A close look at the end of the alphabet shows that someone inscribed an S twice; the second one should look more like an X, according to The Met.

The terracotta cockerel vase was one of several ancient Etruscan artifacts that helped experts partially decode the mysterious ancient language, as it preserved the order of the letters in the early alphabet, archaeologist Gisela Richter wrote in a 1930 catalog of The Met's classical artifacts.

Thanks to the adoption of the Greek alphabet, it's possible to fully sound out the Etruscan language. But although more than 10,000 Etruscan inscriptions have been found, the language is still only partially understood because those inscriptions are short and any lengthy Etruscan literature that once existed has been lost.

#6403. Glue used in batteries makes recycling hard, so engineers designed one that comes off in water

Battery recycling is harder because of the fluorine glue in each cell. A citric acid version dissolves in water and lasted longer in tests.

The glue inside a lithium-ion battery is a tiny share of its weight, yet it shapes how the battery gets built and how hard it is to take it apart for recycling.

In most batteries that glue contains fluorine, and removing it at the end of a battery’s life takes high heat or corrosive chemicals.

However, the new glue is made from two common materials and citric acid, the acid in citrus fruit, and it comes off in plain water.

Test batteries built with it held their charge as well as standard ones, and in extended runs they held it longer. If that holds up at factory scale, the glue would take a toxic solvent out of battery making and simplify recycling.

Engineers at the University of California San Diego developed the glue in Zheng Chen’s Sustainable Materials and Energy Lab. They worked with John Muldoon of Toyota Research Institute of North America and colleagues at Arizona State University.

Every test ran in small lab cells, from watch-battery size up to flat pouches about 1.3 inches (3.3 centimeters) across. Those are far smaller than the packs in electric cars.

Inside a battery, the glue binds a powder that stores charge to a thin metal foil. The standard glue is a fluorine-containing plastic, and it has to be dissolved in a toxic solvent before it can be mixed with that powder.

Once the mix is spread on the foil, big ovens dry the solvent off, and it has to be captured and cleaned for reuse.

Standard-glue electrodes dried off under vacuum at 248°F (120°C) for 12 hours. New-glue electrodes dried in an ordinary oven at 140°F (60°C) for four hours.

“Those extra steps significantly increase the cost and energy use – as well as the environmental impact – of battery manufacturing,” said Jiao Lin, a postdoctoral researcher in Chen’s lab and the study’s first author.

The fluorine glue is also very stable. That helps a battery last, but it means the glue leaves residue that only high heat or harsh chemicals will strip from the material before recycling.

“But that same stability also makes batteries much harder to recycle,” Chen said.

Water-based glues already exist. Carboxymethyl cellulose, a plant-derived thickener found in foods and paper products, holds together the graphite side of some commercial batteries.

On their own, though, glues like this tend to crack as they dry, which leaves the coating brittle. Chen’s team mixed that thickener with polyacrylic acid, a plastic that spreads evenly and bends.

Then they added citric acid, which bonds to both and links them into a single network. Lithium hydroxide kept the mix only mildly acidic, so it wouldn’t corrode the aluminum foil.

The glue made up just 2 percent of each electrode’s weight. Electrodes made with either ingredient alone, or with the two mixed without citric acid, cracked or pulled away from the foil as they dried. The citric acid version dried smooth.

When the team stuck tape on the coating and peeled it off, almost nothing came away. Standard-glue electrodes lost material after only a few peels. The new coating also stayed on when the foil was twisted.

Most test cells used lithium iron phosphate, a battery material that standard recycling methods earn little or no money from. At the start, cells with either glue stored nearly the same charge per gram.

After 1,000 rounds of charging and draining, cells with the new glue had 75.7 percent of their starting capacity. Cells with the standard glue lost capacity faster, especially after about 400 rounds.

So the water-soluble glue didn’t shorten the battery’s working life. In these tests, it added some.

A pouch cell built like a commercial battery, with graphite on the opposite side, kept 76.4 percent of its capacity after 1,600 rounds.

A stack of several layers did a little worse than a single layer, 74.5 percent to 83.5 percent after 700 rounds, which the authors traced to uneven conditions inside the stack.

The glue also worked with other electrode materials, including a nickel-rich one and silicon.

After 100 rounds of use, the team took cells apart. For the standard-glue electrodes, the team used the toxic solvent to lift the coating off.

New-glue electrodes soaked in purified water until the glue dissolved and the coating came cleanly off the foil.

Recovered material from the standard-glue cells still carried fluorine on its surface, left over from the liquid inside the battery. Material from the new-glue cells showed no detectable fluorine.

The team then restored the recovered lithium iron phosphate in a way that keeps it intact instead of breaking it down to raw metals.

Cells built from it kept more of their capacity, and handled fast charging better, than cells built from material recycled out of standard-glue batteries.

Graphite that was recovered in the same way worked again in new cells through 420 rounds.

The team also estimated the environmental cost of a battery cell. By that estimate, building one with the new glue would produce 6.9 percent less greenhouse gas and use 9.3 percent less energy than building one with the fluorine glue.

Recycling it would use 10 percent less energy and release 7.2 percent less greenhouse gas.

The authors call those figures a comparison of scenarios, not measurements from a working plant. The numbers would shift with how much solvent a factory recovers and how it captures fluorine, though the authors say the new glue would still come out ahead.

The new glue doesn’t remove all the fluorine from a battery. The salt in the battery’s liquid contains fluorine too, so the team calculates that the new glue cuts a cell’s total fluorine by about 30 percent.

Lin and Chen are inventors on a patent application for the glue, and Chen’s team plans to commercialize it with industry partners.

Whether the glue works as well when made by the ton and built into full-size batteries is an open question. Scaling up production is the team’s next step, along with adjusting the recipe for other battery types.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6402. Where to Find 15 of Philly's Best Cheesesteaks, According to a Longtime Local

The City of Brotherly Love is filled with meat-and-cheese sandwich lovers. Philadelphia is defined by the big three: Hoagies (loaded Italian and chicken cutlet sandwiches), roast pork (with garlicky broccoli rabe and sharp provolone), and cheesesteaks.

The cheesesteak's story began in the 1930s in South Philadelphia but has become a staple at corner shops across the region, given the gourmet remix by award-winning chefs, and even inspired international outposts in Tokyo and London. I've been eating cheesesteaks since my college days, and as a Philly lifer, I've got plenty of opinions. Consider this your beginner’s guide.

Cheesesteaks are as much a part of Philly's late-night food culture as they are a daytime attraction, especially on weekends and game days. Expect long lines, limited seating, and plenty of takeout orders at popular spots, and bring cash—many old-school shops don't accept cards. Like New York's pizza slice culture, cheesesteaks are typically eaten on the go or at a nearby outdoor table. Grab extra napkins and come hungry.

A classic Philly cheesesteak starts with thinly sliced ribeye steak, melted cheese, and a long Italian roll. But no two shops make it exactly the same, and everyone has their preferences.

The meat: Some shops finely chop their ribeye on the grill, while others leave it in thin slices or longer strips. It comes down to whether you prefer a finely chopped, cheesy mixture or more substantial bites of steak.

The cheese and toppings: American, Cheez Whiz, and provolone are the traditional choices. In Philly, you'll hear people order their preferred cheese "wit" or "without," referring to fried onions. For example, "Whiz wit" means Cheez Whiz with onions, while "American without" means American cheese without onions. Other popular toppings include mushrooms, sweet or hot peppers, which you can often request on the side.

The bread: A good cheesesteak roll is typically long and Italian-style, sometimes seeded, with a lightly crunchy crust and soft interior—similar to New Orleans French bread. Some shops scoop out the excess bread to make more room for the steak and cheese, while others leave the roll intact. Either way, the bread needs to hold up to all that juicy filling.

John's Roast Pork has a signature sandwich of the same name.

John’s on East Snyder Avenue has been a neighborhood fixture for nearly a century, thanks to the Bucci family. The James Beard Award-winning shop has also been voted Best Cheesesteak multiple times, known for its hefty portions of finely chopped, crispy ribeye steak served on crusty rolls sourced from nearby Carangi’s or Sarcone’s. Choose from American, provolone, or Cooper Sharp cheese. Expect long lines, but there’s outdoor seating and a semi-enclosed dining area where you can dig in. And if you’ve got the appetite, don’t leave without trying their signature roast pork sandwich.

You’ve probably heard the hype or seen the long lines on 9th Street. Every cheesesteak at Angelo’s is made with house-baked, crusty bread and fresh, peppery ribeye steak, with your choice of Cooper Sharp or the increasingly popular long-hot-pepper-infused Cheez Whiz. Since its Italian Market debut, the Michelin Bib Gourmand-recognized shop has expanded beyond its Italian Street location, including an outpost at a food hall in Wilmington, Delaware and a ghost kitchen deeper in South Philly, with more locations on the horizon.

400 South St. Philadelphia, PA 19147431 N. 62nd St. Philadelphia, PA 19151

Philadelphia is lucky to have two Jim’s Steaks, each with its own personality. The 50-year-old Jim’s South Street is where all walks of life congregate late into the night, plotting their orders (definitely get the famous Whiz wit), scrambling for cash (there’s an ATM inside that sometimes works), and hollering at motorbikes cruising by. Inside, there’s a first-floor diner-style dining room and a second floor adorned with rare mosaics by the late legendary Philadelphia artist Isaiah Zagar, whose Philadelphia’s Magic Gardens is just a few blocks west. Over in West Philly, Jim’s West—the original location, now under different ownership—sits on a residential corner where O.G.s line up to bring cheesesteaks home to family and friends or score a $20 combo special: a beef or chicken cheesesteak, a drink, and a side of banana pudding.

517 South St. Philadelphia, PA 19147337 South St. Philadelphia, PA 19147

Recently featured in season six of Abbott Elementary, the nearly 50-year-old Ishkabibble’s has long attracted celebrities, locals, and tourists alike, often captured on camera by local photographer South Street Sam. The shop helped popularize chicken cheesesteaks and hot pepper-and-onion Spanish fries, eventually expanding to a second, larger location with additional seating just two blocks away. Chicken cheesesteaks are the name of the game here, with nearly a dozen variations, including Pizza (mozzarella and pizza sauce), South Philly (roasted peppers, spinach, and provolone), and Broccoli (melted cheese and steamed broccoli). Wash it all down with their famous Gremlin, a half-grape soda, half-lemonade concoction. Trust us.

What began as a Northeast Philly corner shop in 1949 has changed owners, locations, and names over the decades, but one thing remains: its signature thinly sliced ribeye cheesesteaks, grilled to order with or without onions on fresh Liscio's rolls delivered daily. In 2013, the renamed shop landed at Fishtown's buzzy corner of Girard and Frankford avenues, transforming into a family-friendly, '50s-style diner with an expanded menu. Alongside its classic cheesesteaks, you'll find vegetarian versions with onions and mushrooms, gluten-free roll options, crinkle-cut fries, egg creams, and sundaes.

1338 S. 10th Street Philadelphia, PA 19147

Got cheesesteak FOMO because you're vegan? Or have plant-based loved ones who want in on the Philly experience? Triangle Tavern, a neighborhood bar on East Passyunk Avenue, has you covered. Most of the menu is vegetarian or vegan, including its only cheesesteak, which was crowned Best Vegan Cheesesteak in Philly by the American Vegan Center in 2019. The winning sandwich features locally owned Blackbird Foods' seitan, fried onions, and a Carangi Bakery roll, all smothered in house-made vegan Whiz (a blend of Daiya vegan cheddar, Tofutti cream cheese, miso, nutritional yeast, and seasonings).

For decades, Robert Perry has cultivated a community of artists, musicians, creatives, and beer lovers at this two-story rock-and-roll bar known for its sticker- and graffiti-covered walls. Affectionately called TMoms by locals, Tattooed Mom welcomes meat lovers and plant-based eaters alike with a savory, gooey vegan cheesesteak. Chunks of seitan and plant-based smoked Gouda replace the traditional steak and Whiz, all tucked into a crusty roll from local bakery Merzbacher's of Germantown. Even better, you can snag one for just $7 on Meatless Mondays.

4540 Baltimore Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19143

A West Philly institution, this husband-and-wife-run Ethiopian restaurant and bar is known for its mashup of East African and Philly staples, particularly its berbere-spiced beef cheesesteaks, served since 1996. Thinly sliced beef is coated in an earthy, fiery blend of chili peppers, coriander, ginger, cardamom, nutmeg, and allspice, then tossed with onions and melted American cheese. The result is a juicy, boldly seasoned cheesesteak with a kick.

1600 W. Girard Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19130

Fairmount may not be the first neighborhood that comes to mind for a Philly cheesesteak, but it's home to an 8,500-square-foot indoor mini golf course serving pan-Asian-inspired bar food. Opened in 2021 by three longtime friends, Libertee Grounds has a playful menu to match, including an Indian-inspired Lamb Kheema cheesesteak made with a masala-rubbed lamb and ribeye blend, melted Cooper Sharp, caramelized onions, and cilantro-lime aioli on a seeded long roll. It comes with fries, but for an extra kick, add pickled Fresno peppers or miso Cooper Sharp cheese Whiz.

3101 Tasker St. Philadelphia, PA 191453401 Walnut St. Franklin's Table Food Hall, Philadelphia, PA 191042563 Trenton Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19125

What began as a food cart in 2022 has grown into multiple Philadelphia locations for Korea Taqueria, where chef-owners Alexander Sherack and Rene Lopez blend traditional Korean flavors with Mexican street food staples. Their Korean-Mexican mashups include a signature slow-burn spicy bulgogi cheesesteak featuring thinly sliced halal ribeye marinated in bulgogi sauce, melted Cooper Sharp, gochujang mayo, and scallions on a seeded Liscio's hoagie roll. Add cucumber kimchi for an extra tangy crunch.

Dalessandro's sits in Roxborough, in the city's northwest outskirts.

Husband-and-wife team Steve and Margie Kotridis have kept this Northwest Philly cheesesteak shop humming with hungry customers since taking over in 2008. Now one of three Michelin Bib Gourmand-recognized cheesesteak shops in Philadelphia, alongside Del Rossi's and Angelo's, Dalessandro's is known for its juicy, gooey, squishy sandwiches. Finely minced ribeye, melted cheese, and generously diced onions meld together inside Amoroso's hearth-baked rolls (another local favorite bakery), which soak up all that goodness. Better yet, toppings are free. Grab your cheesesteak to go and, weather permitting, enjoy it beneath the trees at the park across the street.

3653 Germantown Ave.Philadelphia, PA 19140

This North Philly cheesesteak shop is a celebrity in its own right, having appeared in Creed and Creed II and attracted famous fans like Philly's own Colman Domingo. Since 1994, crowds have lined up beneath its glowing red neon sign near the Broad and Erie transit hub for finely chopped "100% sirloin steak," served in half, whole (12-inch), or Giant (two-foot) portions. Order yours Whiz wit (ketchup is a popular addition here), grab some cheese fries, and join the regulars eating off the hoods of their cars. Those in the know head next door to Eagle Bar for a beer before calling it a night.

3020 S. Broad St. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19145

Heading down to the stadiums for a game? Consider Skinny Joey's your pre- or post-game cheesesteak fix. Former inmate turned podcaster turned restaurateur Joey Merlino has entered Philly's competitive cheesesteak scene, offering six beef and chicken variations that draw long lines of customers and parked cars along Broad Street on weekends. And he's not stopping there: Merlino has expanded to the Jersey Shore with a Wildwood outpost.

Competition and tradition run deep in Philly's cheesesteak scene, a challenge Nish Patel embraced when he took over Del Rossi's in 2020. He helped usher in a new wave of cheesesteak making by focusing on better ingredients and technique rather than reinventing the classic sandwich. First came a house-baked roll with a crunchy crust and pillowy-soft interior. Next, pasture-raised, hormone-free, hand-cut ribeye steak, followed by melted Cooper Sharp American cheese and onions. The upgrades paid off: Del Rossi's earned Michelin Bib Gourmand recognition in 2026.

One of Philly's newest cheesesteak sensations, Sal Burgese's Backyard Cravings began as pandemic-era home cooking for friends, family, and a few lucky guests at his South Philly rowhome. What started in his backyard grew into tailgating parties and, eventually, his first brick-and-mortar shop in October 2026. Like Del Rossi's, the focus here is on quality ingredients and cooking from scratch. The $20+ cheesesteak has a generous portion of finely chopped, salt-and-pepper-seasoned beef, onions, and creamy Cooper Sharp cheese on a long, crisp, sesame-seeded roll with a soft, scooped-out center. Burgese's cheesesteaks have drawn sold-out crowds wherever he's served them, so for now, the Eagles “Kelly Green” and cream-colored corner spot sells them only on weekends.

#6400. A tiny remote controlled beetle robot named BeetleBot uses artificial muscles to explore narrow spaces and grab hidden objects

Printed muscles that shrink when heated let this beetle-sized soft robot walk, grip an object and send back what it feels.

Shrink a walking robot and its motors and gears get harder to fit, not easier. Insect-scale machines have mostly solved this problem with tiny, rigid parts. BeetleBot has neither.

Its legs move because strips of printed plastic shrink when an electric current warms them, the way a muscle shortens when it fires.

The robot is about the size of a real beetle, and a person wearing a sensor patch on one finger steers it by bending that finger.

A camera on its head and a pressure sensor in its jaws send back what it sees and what it is touching. The operator can decide the next move without seeing the robot at all.

Inho Kim built it as a postdoctoral researcher at Caltech and is now an assistant professor of chemistry at Sungkyunkwan University. Sang Ouk Kim of KAIST and Wei Gao of Caltech led the work with a group at NTU Singapore.

The artificial muscles are made of a liquid crystal elastomer, a rubbery plastic with molecules that line up in one direction.

Heat it past a certain point and that alignment breaks down so the material contracts along the line of the molecules and pulls. Let it cool and it stretches back.

The team printed each muscle as a stack of layers with a laser-cut metal heating wire sandwiched inside. Running current through the wire warms the plastic.

At 3 volts, a free-standing muscle shortened by about 45 percent but returned to its full length once the power stopped.

Pulling force matters as much as travel. At their strongest these muscles pulled with 0.18 megapascals of stress. This is within the 0.1 to 0.35 range of a mammal’s skeletal muscle.

That’s why a sheet of printed plastic can carry a robot with a camera and a gripper bolted to it.

The placement of those muscles came from the insect. The team dissected and filmed Mecynorrhina torquata, a large flower beetle, and measured how its leg joints swung when its muscles were stimulated.

That relationship set where the artificial muscles went on the beetle robot’s own six legs.

Insects work their legs with muscles arranged in opposing pairs. One pulls a joint one way and the other pulling it back. BeetleBot copies the arrangement.

Its front legs lift and lower the body, bending about 20 degrees, while the back legs swing forward and back, bending about 12 degrees.

Walking consists of those two groups firing in turn. The front muscles lift the front of the body, which tips the rear legs onto the ground. The back muscles then fold and push the beetle robot forward. Heat one side only and the robot turns.

For the head, the researchers copied the mandibles a beetle uses to hold its prey. Two curved flaps close when their muscles contract, a simpler arrangement than the spring-and-air hand built for the same job. A capacitive pressure sensor sits on the gripping surface.

The sensor is two thin, metal-coated sheets with an air gap between them. Squeeze them closer and the electrical charge they hold changes. This is what the beetle robot reports as contact.

It registered a touch in 0.127 seconds, and its reading rose almost in step with pressure up to 50 kilopascals.

The gripper can also tell shapes apart. Gripping a small sphere, a large sphere and a cube produced three different signal traces. This means the operator learns something about the object without ever seeing it close up.

A perching drone reads a branch the same way, by touch, where a camera stops helping.

The control patch is a printed strip of rubbery polymer loaded with carbon nanotubes, tiny conductive threads that form a network through the material.

Bending the finger stretches the strip, breaks some of those connections, and raises its electrical resistance.

Four finger movements produced four clearly separated signals, which the system reads as forward, left, right and grip, then sends to the robot over a short-range, wireless link. The patch held its signal through 1,000 bending cycles.

“A key feature of this work is the bidirectional feedback, which links the information detected by the robot to the user’s next action,” said Inho Kim, the paper’s first author.

Information running both ways is what separates this beetle robot from a remote-control toy. Other soft machines go further still, thinking without electricity by building the logic into the material itself.

The person sends a gesture, the robot sends back a camera frame and a pressure reading, and the next gesture depends on what came back.

To test all of it together, the team set a target object behind an obstacle and had an operator drive the robot there using the camera feed alone.

It took eight separate movements, turns and forward runs in sequence, to get around the obstacle, reach the object, close the gripper on it and carry it.

The pressure signal jumped at the moment of contact, which is how the operator knew to grip. That is the whole loop in one run: a finger moves, legs move, a sensor answers, and the finger moves again.

“This study expands the potential uses of soft robots by connecting the movement of artificial muscles, sensing, and user control in a single system,” said Sang Ouk Kim.

The muscles only work hot. Full contraction needs the plastic above roughly 230°F (110°C), and surfaces on the robot climbed past 212°F (100°C) during walking.

A thermal camera showed that heat staying local to the working muscle rather than spreading through the frame.

Heat is also what sets the pace. Each step waits for the plastic to cool, so the walking cycle runs slower than the muscle’s own limit. Adding payload slowed it further.

Two other limits stand in the way of sending one of these somewhere real. The finger patch’s signals pass through a wired front end before they go wireless, and the course the robot crossed was a small, built setup, not rubble or a pipe.

KAIST said the actuation speed, the energy efficiency and the power supply all need work before soft robots like this one inspect industrial equipment or explore the environment.

Nobody has driven one of these through a space that a person could not enter. Inho Kim said he plans to make the muscles faster and more efficient, and to improve the control methods that use the robot’s own sensing.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6399. Scientists found a hidden ‘aging clock’ in human blood that can predict future diseases and early death

Scientists have figured out a new way to measure how fast your body is actually aging on the inside, rather than just counting the years you have been alive.

Two people born the same year can have bodies that age at different speeds. A routine blood draw may now be enough to tell which is which.

In a study of 18,476 people aged 1 to 96, some had blood chemistry that read older than their birth certificate. Those people went on to develop fatty liver disease, high blood pressure and diabetes more often.

More of them died over the following years, too.

The older readings lined up with everyday habits. Smokers’ blood read about 1.2 years older than nonsmokers’, and people who exercised read about half a year younger.

Linlin Cao, Kun Qian, Jun Pu and Wei Xu of Renji Hospital at Shanghai Jiao Tong University led the study, with participants from six clinical centers in China. It’s observational, so it shows patterns, not causes.

Blood plasma carries thousands of small molecules left over from the body’s chemistry. The field that measures them is called metabolomics.

The team measured 232 of these molecules, in each person, with a laser-based instrument that needs a droplet of plasma and about 30 seconds per sample.

From those, 56 molecules changed most reliably with age. Some rose steadily, such as creatinine, a waste product of muscle.

Others fell early in life and stayed low, such as a building block of collagen that was highest in childhood and dropped fast before age 20.

A set of 12 machine learning models, stacked together, used the 56 molecules to guess each person’s age. The guesses were close.

In 5,252 healthy people used for training, the guess landed within about two years on average. In 5,456 healthy people held back as a test, it landed within about 4.5 years.

The difference between that guess and a person’s real age is the number that matters. The team called it metabolomic age acceleration, and a positive value means the blood reads older than the calendar.

Everyone gave blood in 2019. The healthy participants answered a questionnaire on diet, sleep, smoking, exercise and family history, and 3,745 of them returned for a health check in 2023. Deaths were tracked through January 2025.

The team compared the quarter of healthy people with the most accelerated blood chemistry against the quarter with the slowest.

The accelerated quarter had more new cases of fatty liver disease, high blood pressure and diabetes, and the same held for coronary heart disease and stroke.

The accelerated quarter also died at a higher rate. There were 291 deaths among the 6,169 people with death records, and the accelerated quarter accounted for a larger share of them.

For predicting death, the blood clock edged out two standard yardsticks, a frailty index and the American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 score. It also added information when combined with them.

People of the same age can follow different aging paths, and this is one way to see it.

Several habits lined up with the clock. Current smoking was associated with blood chemistry about 1.2 years older, secondhand smoke with about 0.6 years, shift work with about 0.9 years, and hair dye with about a year.

Sugar, fried food, processed meat and organ meat were also associated with an older reading. Exercise was associated with a reading about half a year younger, and mixed grains with about a third of a year younger.

In 1,500 people who gave blood again in 2023, the clock moved with their habits. Those who became more active or ate less fried food saw their blood chemistry read younger by two to three years.

People newly exposed to secondhand smoke, eating more preserved food, or crossing into overweight saw it read older. The authors wrote that these habit links are observational and shouldn’t be read as causes.

Other studies have tied biological aging to teenage body weight, early menopause and even the time between pregnancies. Air pollution also leaves a chemical trail in the blood.

In 7,768 people who already had a chronic disease, the age guess worked less well, so the team built a different measure.

Using the same 56 molecules, they modeled each person’s risk of death and then asked how far it sat above or below what their age would predict.

They called that age deviation. Eight molecules carried the death signal, and the strongest was 3-methylindole, made by gut microbes from the amino acid tryptophan. The collagen building block, 4-hydroxyproline, pointed the other way, toward lower risk.

Higher age deviation went with worse kidney numbers, more organ systems affected and more conditions at once. Chronic kidney disease had the largest link.

People with high blood pressure who got it under control by 2023 saw their age deviation improve more than those who didn’t.

Nearly everyone in the study was Chinese, so the clock needs testing in other populations before it travels. Most people gave blood only once, and the authors wrote that more frequent sampling and longer follow-up are needed.

The identities of some of the 56 molecules are confident matches rather than certainties.

The open question is whether changing a habit to move the clock changes what happens to a person afterward. The authors wrote that intervention studies would be needed to find this out.

The age-prediction tool, called MetS-Age, is public for researchers to run on their own data.

The full study was published in the journal Science Translational Medicine.

#6397. I Visited China as an American Without a Visa—Here’s How You Can Do It Too

Last month, I visited China as an American—without going through a multi-week visa application process. This is thanks to a recent policy introduced in 2024 that allows certain travelers to visit China for a maximum of 10 days while transiting between one country and another. Though the rule can feel intimidating in theory, it’s relatively straightforward in practice as long as you prepare accordingly.

Officially called the “240-Hour Visa-Free Transit Policy," the program is part of China’s goal to attract more inbound international travelers, according to Mei Zhang, the founder of WildChina and a Condé Nast Traveler travel specialist. “The idea is to make visiting China an easier decision,” Zhang says. “Most people are daunted by the idea of queuing for a visa at the Chinese consulate. Removing that step makes it easier for people to come.”

And even though the policy is designed for transiting between countries, 10 days is still enough time for a meaningful visit. “Beyond the quick business visits or short stopovers people may associate with China, ten days gives travelers time to explore several destinations, experience the culture, and develop a deeper appreciation for the country,” says Catherine Heald, CNT specialist and founder of Remote Lands, which specializes in travel to Asia.

However, because the program is relatively new, not all airline or airport staff are familiar with it—which almost resulted in me being denied boarding. To help you avoid ending up in a similar situation, here’s what travelers should know before booking your flight to China, so you too can see the Forbidden City in Beijing, the futuristic skyline glowing along the Bund in Shanghai, the terracotta warriors in Xi'an, and the mountainous megacity of Chongqing.

Officially called the “240-Hour Visa-Free Transit Policy,” this new rule was first introduced by China’s National Immigration Administration in December 2024. It permits a traveler to visit China without obtaining a visa ahead of time as long as the total length of their stay in the country does not exceed 240 hours. “It’s a great policy that has driven the growth of international travelers to China,” says Zhang, “but you do need to read the fine print before using it.”

The fine print: First of all, the operative word is transit. You have to enter China from one country, then leave it for another, different country. For example, flying from the US to China, then from China to Japan is allowed. However, going from the US to China, then back to the US, is not. Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan count as separate destinations for this policy, so a trip that goes from Hong Kong to mainland China to Taiwan would qualify for a visa-free transit in China that does not last longer than 10 days.

Second: Only holders of passports from 57 countries, including the United States, can take advantage of this policy. See the full list here. And third: You have to enter and exit via designated ports. The full list is here, and it conveniently includes the cities you might visit on a first-time visit to China, like Beijing, Shanghai, and Chengdu. If you want to travel beyond the areas permitted by the transit policy, you’ll have to apply for a Chinese visa.

“Remember that you can enter and leave through the same eligible Chinese city or choose different eligible cities,” says Heald of Remote Lands. So you could come to China through Shanghai, spend three days there, then take the high-speed train to Beijing, stay for another three days, then depart for a third destination like nearby South Korea to make the most out of your trip.

The Forbidden City was the Chinese imperial palace from the Ming dynasty to the end of the Qing dynasty (1420-1912).

To try the transit policy for myself, I kept my first-ever trip to China simple. I arrived in Shanghai on September 30 and departed on October 5, entering and exiting through the same qualifying port, Shanghai Pudong International Airport (PVG). I stayed in the country for a total of five nights, well under the 240-hour limit. (For what it’s worth, I stayed at the good-looking PuLi Shanghai, the very cool Upper House Shanghai, and the historically rich Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li, to explore different parts of the city.)

I’m an American citizen, so my US passport made me eligible for the transit policy. As for my routing, I departed from Paris, where I live, on a direct flight to Shanghai; from there I flew onward to Manila. The logic is that this made my visit to China count as a long layover since my final destination was actually the Philippines.

As you prepare your itinerary, check—and double check—that your passport, routing, entry and departure ports in China, and destinations within China all qualify under the 240-hour visa-free transit policy before you make your bookings. The list of qualifying passports and entry-exit ports in China can be found here.

Once you have all your confirmation info, it’s a good idea to get organized and put together a folder with all your bookings as proof of your plans to stay no more than 10 days in China. “Carry printed copies of your confirmed onward tickets, hotel reservations, and itinerary,” Heald says. She also recommends calling your airline before departure and confirming your transit eligibility with them. You might even print the official page describing the policy (again, here!) so you can present it to anyone you encounter, like a check-in agent, who might be unfamiliar with the relatively new 10-day rule.

Consider this your heads up, says Zhang: “It’s a great policy but sometimes the implementation on the ground can be uneven.” For an added layer of security, consider booking your travel to China with local tour operators or travel specialists like WildChina or Remote Lands. They can design a trip that will definitely qualify for the transit policy, and can help you out in case you run into issues while you’re traveling.

Well, I did none of the above. I arrived at Paris-Charles de Gaulle for my flight to Shanghai without any printed confirmations of my onward ticket to Manila, my three hotel stays, or the official policy from the Chinese National Immigration Administration’s official website.

The Air France check-in agent asked me to present my Chinese visa, which, of course, I did not have. I tried to explain in French that I could go to China through this new policy, but the agent insisted, “Non, c’est pas possible.” Foolishly, I plugged “10-day visa-free transit China” into Google on my phone and presented the results to him. He sighed, switched to English, and said, “That is not official. That is AI Overview.”

I asked if there was anyone at Air France I could talk to, and the agent shook his head. Maybe he softened when he saw the panic creep across my face because he then phoned a colleague, an Air France agent who was Chinese. The other agent explained that I was correct, there is indeed a new 10-day transit policy, and all I had to do was present my onward ticket to the Philippines, which I did have saved as a screenshot on my phone.

May my failure to properly prepare be your reminder to print out everything, including your flight and accommodation info, as well as the official visa-free transit policy. If there was ever a time to be a type-A traveler, it’s this.

Once in China, the process becomes much smoother. All international travelers are required to fill out a digital arrival form, whether they have a visa or not. The form asks if you have a visa for China and, when you select no, offers a drop-down menu where you can declare that you are visiting through the 240-hour visa-free transit policy. Once that’s done, the form gives you a QR code that confirms you’ve completed the form; screenshot this code, just in case. Then go through the immigration line, approach the immigration officer, and present whatever is asked of you, like that QR code or your onward ticket, when prompted. That’s it!

For my journey, I got to Pudong Airport in Shanghai, logged onto the airport Wi-Fi, completed the form, and went into the immigration line. They didn’t ask for the QR code but they did ask for my ticket to Manila. Once everything looked good to them, they stamped my passport with a transit visa—a little sticker that declared my date of entry into China and when they expected me to leave. I was cleared to go, and I stepped into the duty-free shopping area, located right before baggage claim, feeling giddy and satisfied that it all worked out.

Zhang says working with a travel company could help relieve some of the stress on the arrival side too: “WildChina normally would book a VIP airport pickup if any of our travelers are using the 10-day transit visa. This way, an airport concierge would meet the guests at the gate and walk them through the visa step-by-step. This eases the stress of facing an unfamiliar bureaucratic process.”

One of the things that greatly intimidated me about visiting China was how different the tech is. There’s no Uber or Google Maps, which has been very helpful for me on my solo travels in new-to-me countries. The very fine teams at PuLi Shanghai and Upper House Shanghai helped me get set up with the right apps, and I was zipping around the city in no time. (For a map app, Apple Maps worked like a charm, to my surprise.) Here are tips for what Chinese apps to download before traveling.

First, set up Alipay, which is a do-it-all app and a total lifeline in China. You can link an international bank card and use it for all payments everywhere you go; call a DiDi car (China’s equivalent of Uber or Lyft), use its translation tool, and more. “Alipay is part of everyday life here,” Zhang says. “At most restaurants, you can scan the QR code on your table with Alipay, choose your dishes—already translated on the interface—and pay through the app.” Be sure to set it up and link your bank account or card before you arrive in China; some verification steps require authorization via your phone number, which you may not have access to while in the country.

Second, everyone in China is on WeChat, so you’d do well to download that too; it’s how I communicated with the guest experiences team at Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li, who took me on cultural tours in the hotel’s neighborhood. Think of it as Chinese WhatsApp.

And to stay connected online, Heald suggests checking if your existing carrier offers roaming in mainland China (helpful for any verification texts you may need to receive). Otherwise, get a compatible travel eSIM that explicitly covers it. A home carrier or a travel eSIM will allow you to connect to sites like Google Workplace and apps like Instagram that you would not be able to normally access through the internet while in China. For my phone, Airalo, a travel eSIM, and Free, my French home carrier, worked perfectly.

“If you'll be using a laptop or tablet on Wi-Fi and need access to services such as Google, WhatsApp, or Instagram, install a VPN and arrange any paid subscription before you leave,” Zhang says. “Downloading and setting it up can be much trickier once you're in China.” I, for one, used Astrill VPN to stay connected on my laptop to sites like Gmail and YouTube.

And finally, both Zhang and Heald recommend keeping an open mind. “China can feel very different from what you know,” Heald says. “Give yourself the chance to observe, ask questions and learn, rather than expecting everything to feel familiar.” Zhang adds, “That's part of getting to know a place. Don’t be afraid to ask for help or start a conversation, even if you only have a few words in common. You'll often find people are curious about you too, and pleased that you've come to see where they live.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6396. Researchers proved that tiny lab-grown brains can process information and read Braille just like a real computer

Three brain organoids read Braille letters far better than one, and the living tissue held up even when researchers damaged the data.

Could a computer one day run on living brain cells instead of silicon? A small experiment has just given that question a plain, partial answer.

Specks of human brain tissue, known as organoids, were grown in a dish in a lab. They received the shapes of Braille letters as electrical pulses, and a program read the letters back from how the cells fired.

One speck got the letter right about 61 percent of the time. Three specks, with their signals combined, got it right 83 percent of the time.

Tianyi Liu, a doctoral student at the University of Bristol, led the work with Hemma Philamore and Benjamin Ward-Cherrier in the University’s School of Engineering Mathematics and Technology.

The brain organoids are clumps of human neurons and support cells grown in a lab. Each is about a fiftieth of an inch (half a millimeter) across, the width of a mechanical pencil’s lead.

Nothing in this experiment learned anything, and that matters for how far the result reaches.

“We can take information from a real tactile sensor, turn it into a form that a living neural network can receive, and then recover meaningful information from the organoid response,” said Liu.

“That gives us a practical way to connect artificial sensors with biological neural systems, which are a very interesting possible route towards more energy-efficient computing,” she added.

The attraction is power. A human brain runs on roughly 20 watts. Silicon brain-inspired chips scaled up to the size of a cortex would need kilowatts to megawatts, the team wrote.

Other labs have already had lab-grown brain cells tell Japanese vowels apart and play a simple video game.

The brain organoids never touched a Braille dot. A touch sensor did that for them. The team mounted a sensor with a soft silicone pad, a kind of electronic skin, on a small robot arm.

The arm slid the pad across each of the 26 letters on a 3D-printed Braille board about 9 inches by 5.5 inches (23 by 14 centimeters).

A camera inside the pad recorded tiny shifts in a grid of markers as the dots pressed into the gel, the way a robot fingertip gets its sense of touch. Each letter was scanned 10 times at each of five pressing depths, 1,300 recordings in all.

The team split each recording into eight regions, one for each electrode under an organoid. The touch in each region then became a train of electric pulses.

More contact in a region meant more pulses, between four and ten, and a longer contact meant longer pulses.

The organoids live on electrode arrays run by a company called FinalSpark, and the team reached them over the internet. Kept under a steady flow of nutrient liquid, an organoid can stay electrically active for up to about 100 days.

For each letter, the team counted the cells’ firing on each of the eight electrodes for half a second after the pulses arrived. A standard pattern-sorting program then learned which firing patterns went with which letter.

With a single organoid, the program named the right letter about 61 percent of the time, where guessing would get just under 4 percent right.

Three organoids on the same array, each read on its own, scored 59, 62 and 67 percent. Combined into one pattern, the three organoids’ signals lifted the score to 83 percent.

So the gain didn’t come from one unusually good organoid. It came from combining them.

Why that works isn’t settled. The team’s best guess is that the three organoids differ slightly, so each one transforms the same input a little differently. The program then gets three partly different views of one letter.

“Different organoids may have slightly different network connections, developmental states, and ongoing activity, so the same input can produce similar but not identical responses,” Liu said.

“Combining those responses may give us complementary information that we would not get from a single organoid. At the same time, if every organoid behaves differently, it obviously makes it harder to build a predictable and standardized system,” she added.

There was an obvious objection. The pulse patterns were designed to preserve each letter’s shape, so maybe the program was reading the team’s own encoding and the tissue was only passing it along.

The team tested that directly. Given the pulse patterns with no organoid in between, the same program scored 82 percent, almost exactly the three-organoid result. On a clean signal, the organoids made almost no difference.

Then the team corrupted half of the channels in four ways: two kinds of random noise, some entries set to zero, and some values tripled. Reading straight from the pulses, the program fell to between 55 and 67 percent.

Reading from the three organoids, it held at 83 and 82 percent under random noise, and fell to 72 and 68 percent when entries went missing or were tripled.

In every one of the four tests, the organoids came out ahead. That, more than the headline score, is the contribution the team claims for the living tissue. Ward-Cherrier, the senior author, summed up the two results.

“After processing by the organoids, the tactile data still contains enough information to classify Braille letters with good accuracy. Combining outputs from several organoids also showed an improvement in performance.”

The signal in this experiment ran one way. Pulses went in, firing came out, and nothing went back to the tissue to say whether it had been right. No organoid got feedback, so none could get better with practice.

“We showed that tactile information could be encoded, processed through the organoids, and decoded, but we did not demonstrate learning or long-term changes in the organoids,” Liu said.

“We also tested one tactile task using a fixed encoding scheme and a relatively simple measure of neural activity.”

Eight electrodes per organoid is also a coarse view of a clump of cells, too coarse to see fine patterns in the firing.

And the team hasn’t measured how alike the three organoids’ responses are, which would show whether they carry different information or three copies of it. Whether a fourth organoid would help is also untested.

In 2024, a robot with a camera in its fingertip read Braille faster than a person can, and nothing here beats that.

The question this study asks is different: whether living tissue can hold a job inside a machine, and do it on a fraction of the power.

In the next experiments, the team plans to give the organoids textures and edges to feel, and then feedback on what they do with them.

Only then can anyone ask whether this tissue can learn.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence.

In a key coastal area of Peru, violence was low despite the practice of human sacrifice.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Despite engaging in human sacrifice, the people who lived in the Lambayeque Valley of northern Peru had low levels of violence, a new study of their remains finds.

Human sacrifice occurred in the valley over the millennia. It's thought that at least some of these mass sacrifices were attempts to appease the gods in the wake of El Niño, a periodic weather phenomenon that can lead to intense rains and flooding in Peru and droughts in other parts of South and Central America.

"We have one example at the site of Sicán where around [A.D.] 1050/1100, around 200 individuals were killed and ritualistically buried during an intense El Niño event," study co-author Haagen Klaus, an anthropology professor at George Mason University in Virginia, told Live Science in an email.

Other human sacrifice findings include more than 200 children found near the modern-day town of Huanchaco who were sacrificed sometime between 600 and 800 years ago, possibly during an El Niño.

However, despite the occurrence of human sacrifice, levels of violence unrelated to sacrifice were actually quite low in the Lambayeque Valley. In the study, scientists analyzed the skeletal remains of 1,519 people from the Lambayeque Valley who lived between roughly 1500 B.C. and A.D. 1800, and whose remains were preserved enough to detect signs of violent trauma, including interpersonal violence.

A skull showing blunt force trauma that dates to the Chimu period, roughly 1375 to 1490.

Of these skeletons, "only 25 (1.6%) exhibited traumatic lesions consistent with interpersonal conflict, and 77 exhibited post-cranial traumatic lesions consistent with accidental trauma (5.1%)," Klaus and co-author Thomas Snyder, a bioarchaeologist at New York University, wrote in the paper, which was published Nov. 8 in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

The team didn't find any link between a person's sex and violence, they noted. The findings mean that despite the presence of human sacrifice, the amount of violence unrelated to sacrifice was low. This leaves a question: Why?

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A healed fracture on the left leg of a person who lived sometime between 1000 to 650 B.C. The fracture may have been from an accident.

"Ritual violence may have alleviated non-ritual violence by creating spaces where social tensions could get worked out in a few different ways," Klaus said.

It's important to remember that other areas of Peru also practiced human sacrifice but didn't have the same low levels of interpersonal violence. Klaus noted that areas in the Peruvian highlands sometimes had higher rates of interpersonal violence. In their paper, Klaus and Snyder noted that societies that originated in the highlands, such as the Tiwanaku, Wari and Inca had to grapple with poorer soils and cold temperatures, and these challenges may have been a factor in increasing the levels of interpersonal violence.

The "evidence of sub-lethal and lethal violence forceful enough to break bone is significantly higher in some areas of Peru's highlands," Klaus said. He and Snyder noted in their paper that the inhabitants of the Lambayeque Valley may have had better access to marine and water resources, such as seafood and rivers that could be used for agricultural irrigation, than those who lived in highland areas. Access to these resources may have helped alleviate interpersonal violence in the valley by providing more food resources, they wrote.

Aside from practicing human sacrifice, people in the valley may have engaged in other practices that helped lower levels of interpersonal violence, researchers who were not involved in the new study told Live Science.

Environmental conditions may have helped reduce conflict or there could be "really unusual cultural practices in this region of avoiding or mediating conflict — both between and within groups," Elizabeth Arkush, an anthropology professor at the University of Pittsburgh, said in an email.

Constanza Ceruti, an anthropologist and explorer with the National Geographic Society, said in an email that she's glad that researchers are studying human sacrifices "after decades of being ignored as a taboo topic in academic discussion." She praised the study’s large sample size and noted that human sacrifice is a "phenomenon primarily associated [with] the manipulation and concentration of power by elites."

Jordi Rivera Prince, an anthropology professor at Tulane University, said that the findings dovetail with her excavations in the region, where she has "found little evidence of violent trauma during the Salinar (400-200 BCE), a period of great social change in the Andes."

Weston McCool, an archaeology professor at Cal Poly, said in an email that the newly published paper "is an interesting study that provides additional evidence for a sharp break in patterns of violence between the Andean coast and highlands." He noted that it "supports the hypothesis that coastal populations were buffered from terrestrial environmental downturns in ways that highland populations were not. The nature of that resilience, however, remains an important question for future research."

Snyder, T. J., & Klaus, H. D. (2026). Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru. Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, 5, 1889466. https://doi.org/10.3389/fearc.2026.1889466

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6393. Jellyfish study shows scientists that evolution may be ‘much more predictable than we expected’

A new study reveals unrelated jellyfish evolved identical genetic mutations, but surprisingly, these matching DNA changes did not result in matching physical traits.

Biologists have always assumed that it is incredibly rare for two different species to independently develop the exact same genetic changes after being separated for millions of years.

However, a new study looking at the DNA of ancient jellyfish shows that evolution repeats itself much more than scientists ever realized.

Across 86 species, lineages that split more than 600 million years ago have repeatedly swapped in the same building block at the same spot in the same protein. It happened far more often than pure chance would allow.

The twist is what those shared changes are not. They mostly have nothing to do with the traits the animals visibly share, such as eyes.

Cory Berger, a postdoctoral researcher in Todd Oakley’s lab at UC Santa Barbara, led the work. Colleagues at the University of Kansas, Texas A&M University and the University of Nebraska took part.

Everything here comes from comparing gene sequences across species; no trait was tested in a lab.

“We’re studying molecular evolution here – to what extent similar genetic changes occur in different organisms,” Berger said. “And that in particular is something we don’t know much about.”

The group the team chose, called Medusozoa, takes in the true jellyfish, box jellyfish and the hydroids, which are small branching animals related to them. The team’s dating, anchored by 17 fossils, puts the origin of the group at about 685 million years ago.

Before anyone could compare genes, the team had to know who was related to whom and when they split.

They built a tree of 621 species, anchored by the full gene sets of 98 of them, 22 sequenced for this study, and then traced three traits across it.

The results show how often evolution repeats at the level of the body, a pattern biologists call convergent evolution. Eyes, for example, arose at least nine separate times.

The free-swimming medusa stage, the bell-shaped adult most people picture, was lost 41 times. Colonies switched from crusts to upright branching forms 32 times.

“Maybe it’s just the case that organisms that have phenotypic convergence who look similar to one another have convergent molecular changes,” Berger said, describing the idea the team set out to test.

The team compared the protein-coding genes of the 86 species, two at a time. This meant 3,570 pairs were compared, across 9,194 gene families.

For each pair, it looked for spots where both lineages had independently changed the same amino acid, one of the building blocks of a protein, to the same new one.

“And then we looked at the patterns of change across those genes. If the same specific change has happened in distantly related species, then we’re calling that convergence,” said Oakley, the senior author.

The team found 426,322 such matches, under a tenth of a percent of all the branch pairs it tested, and they appeared in 8,991 of the 9,194 gene families.

At those spots, the new amino acid also tended to differ more in its chemistry from the old one than at other changed spots in the same proteins. The team reads that pattern as natural selection rather than accident.

Matches did get rarer as the time since two species split grew longer. But the decline was gentle, and even pairs separated by more than 600 million years shared more changes than a model of pure chance predicted.

If evolution reuses genes to build the same trait, species that both evolved eyes, or both lost the medusa stage, should share more genetic changes than other pairs. They didn’t. Pairs with a shared trait were statistically indistinguishable from pairs without one.

Genes known to help build eyes did show up a little more often among eye-bearing pairs. But the same genes had also been under the same kind of selection in species with no eyes at all.

What did set the convergent genes apart was their job.

Genes that deal with the outside world, including energy metabolism, immune defense and breaking down foreign chemicals, carried the most repeated changes. Genes that run the cell’s internal housekeeping, such as cell division, carried the fewest.

“The amount of genetic similarity indicates that at the genetic level, evolution may be more repeatable and maybe therefore more predictable than we expected,” Oakley said.

“But it also means that we still have a huge amount to learn about how the genes function, how that plays out on the whole-organism scale.”

The team counted only one kind of genetic change, a swap of one amino acid for another. Changes in the DNA that switches genes on and off, which may matter more for body shape, were not part of the analysis.

Also, genes facing the environment may simply evolve faster, which would give them more chances to match.

The bigger gap is the cause. For most shared genetic changes, the pressure that drove them in both lineages is unknown.

The team’s own example of a solved case is a pump found in cell membranes. It evolved separately in amphibians, reptiles, mammals and insects to resist the same heart toxins, made by toads and by plants. There, the shared diet explains the shared gene.

The jellyfish data suggest many cases like that are waiting, each with its own explanation. Finding them means measuring the pressures these animals face in the sea as carefully as the team has now measured their genes.

That, the authors wrote, is the next job.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
